### Why doesn't it happen?

⏱️

**Short-term funding cycles**
Public health grant announced with weeks' notice. Prevention needs 5–10 year horizons.

📊

**No universal definition**
ICBs can't baseline current prevention spend, the [Hewitt Review (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-hewitt-review-an-independent-review-of-integrated-care-systems) found developing one will take "several years".

🎯

**Performance pressure**
ICBs judged on waiting lists and financial balance. Prevention doesn't show up in next quarter's metrics.

💰

**Treasury wants "cashable savings"**
Even with strong business cases, finance teams resist "jam tomorrow". The Green Book supports DALYs, but practice lags.

### What's changing

*   **[10 Year Health Plan (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/10-year-health-plan-for-england-fit-for-the-future)**: commits to "prevention accelerators" in selected ICBs, with focus on CVD and diabetes
*   **[Hewitt Review (2023) (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-hewitt-review-an-independent-review-of-integrated-care-systems) implementation**, DHSC and NHSE developing a prevention spend definition for baselining, as the Review recommended
*   **Recommendation**: increase NHS prevention spend by at least 1% of ICB budgets over 5 years (ideally 10–20% long-term)
*   **Shift from hospital to home**, Better Care Fund and DFG supporting housing-based prevention

## The bottom line

We asked: **how is health spending structured, and why does it keep growing?**

### Three channels, different equity implications

**Government transfers** dominate in the UK at 81%, among the highest globally. This is the NHS model: tax-funded, free at point of use, risk pooled across the population.

**Social insurance** (Germany, France) achieves similar coverage through employer/employee contributions but with higher administrative complexity.

**Out-of-pocket** exceeds 40% in many LMICs, creating real barriers. The UK's 14.1% OOP is a genuine strength, reducing it further is central to universal coverage globally.

Growth

+1.5%

### Structural forces, not policy failure

Five forces drive spending upward everywhere: **population growth**, **demographic ageing**, **chronic disease burden**, **medical technology**: and **workforce costs** that outpace productivity.

Healthcare can't easily automate, a phenomenon economists call "Baumol's cost disease." OECD's central projection has public spending on health rising by a further **+1.5% of GDP by 2045** across OECD countries (OECD, _Health at a Glance 2025_); the exact pace depends on demographic, productivity, and technology assumptions.

The question isn't _whether_ to spend more. It's whether that spending translates into proportionate health gains.

prevention

### More spending ≠ better outcomes

The US spends 17.2% of GDP yet has the **lowest life expectancy** among peers (78.4 years). Japan spends 10.6% and has the highest (84.1 years). The relationship isn't linear.

What matters is _how_ money is spent. The ringfenced Public Health Grant is just **0.3% of total government spending**, cut 26% per person in real terms since 2015/16, despite a [median £14:£1 return (opens in new tab)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5537512/) across public health interventions (Masters et al. 2017).

We're treating illness, not preventing it. Every prevention business case has to overcome this structural bias toward acute care.

The real question isn't

"How much should we spend?"

It's

"How do we turn spending into health?"

### For practitioners

If you're making investment decisions in the NHS or advising on health system reform, three priorities emerge:

*   **Focus on value, not volume**: build cases around efficiency and evidence-based allocation, not just more spending
*   **Protect pooled financing**: rising OOP erodes equity; the NHS model has genuine strengths worth defending
*   **Make the case for prevention**: the ROI is there, but you'll need frameworks like the [Green Book (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-green-book-appraisal-and-evaluation-in-central-government) to overcome institutional bias

## Health expenditure: key questions answered

How much does the UK spend on healthcare?

The UK spent £345bn on healthcare in 2025 (provisional), equivalent to 11.4% of GDP on current health expenditure — the internationally comparable measure. Source: ONS UK Health Accounts 2025, OECD Health at a Glance 2025.

How does UK health spending vary internationally?

The UK ranks mid-table among high-income countries. The US spends 17.2% of GDP, Germany 12.3%, France 11.5%, the UK 11.4% (ONS 2025 provisional; 11.1% on the OECD basis), and Japan 10.6%. Among G7 nations, only Japan and Italy (8.4%) spend a smaller share on the consistent OECD basis. Source: OECD Health at a Glance 2025; ONS UK Health Accounts 2025.

What percentage of GDP does the UK spend on health?

11.4% of GDP on current health expenditure (2025 provisional). High-income countries range from around 8% to 17% of GDP, with most between 9% and 13%. Source: ONS UK Health Accounts, OECD Health at a Glance 2025.

Who pays for healthcare in the UK?

Government funds 81% of UK health spending (£280bn of £345bn), high by international standards where high-income countries average around 60%. Out-of-pocket expenditure accounts for 14.1% (£48.5bn), covering prescriptions, dental care, and private treatments. Voluntary health insurance has been the fastest-growing component (up 13.8% in real terms in 2024). Source: ONS UK Health Accounts 2025.

How much does the UK spend on public health and prevention?

Three measures with different numerators, denominators and vintages, so they are not directly comparable: **5%** of UK government health spending on the narrow ONS preventive-care category (£12.2bn of £269.1bn in 2024, ONS); **5.6%** of total current health expenditure on the broader OECD HC.6 preventive-care definition (a wider numerator covering health-protection, disease-prevention, health-promotion and surveillance); and the ringfenced Public Health Grant at just **0.3%** of total government spending (all departments). Prevention spending nearly quadrupled during COVID-19 but has since fallen back, partly a classification artefact (pandemic response was recorded as preventive care). Evidence suggests a median £14:£1 return across public health interventions (local-intervention median is £4:£1, the more decision-relevant figure for ICBs). Source: ONS UK Health Accounts 2025, OECD Health at a Glance 2025, Masters et al. 2017.

What is driving health spending growth?

Five structural forces drive health spending growth globally: population growth (9.7bn projected by 2050), demographic ageing (healthcare costs peak at end of life), rising non-communicable diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer), medical technology advances (new treatments at higher cost), and workforce costs (healthcare is labour-intensive). Public spending on health is projected to rise by a further +1.5% of GDP by 2045 on OECD's central projection. Source: OECD, Health at a Glance 2025.

How much do countries spend on mental health?

Most OECD countries spend well below the recommended 10% of health budgets on mental health. France leads at 15%, and only five countries — the UK, Canada, Germany, Norway and France — reported spending above 10% in the OECD's 2021 benchmarking (the UK value is England data). On the narrower NHS measure, the UK allocates around 8.78% of ICB baseline funding to mental health (2024/25). Mental ill-health costs OECD economies more than 4% of GDP, in the UK alone, the societal cost is estimated at £118bn per year. Source: OECD A New Benchmark for Mental Health Systems (2021, CC BY 4.0), NHS MH Dashboard, LSE/MHF (2022).

Focused Question

## How is health spending structured, and why does it keep growing?

Health expenditure is one of the largest categories of public spending in most developed economies. In the UK, we spend **£345bn** on healthcare annually, **11.4% of GDP**. But where does that money actually come from? Who decides how it's allocated? And what forces are pushing spending ever upward?

Understanding these fundamentals is essential for anyone working in health economics, commissioning, or service planning. This briefing breaks down the structure of health financing, from global patterns to UK-specific flows, and examines the drivers that make health spending one of the fastest-growing components of government budgets worldwide.

Across OECD countries, health spending continues to outpace overall GDP growth. OECD's central projection sees public spending on health rising by an additional **1.5% of GDP by 2045**: driven by technological change, rising expectations of what healthcare can achieve, and population ageing (OECD, _Health at a Glance 2025_, CC BY 4.0). The question isn't whether spending will keep rising, but whether that growth translates into proportionate improvements in health outcomes.

For UK-specific context, explore the [Health System Hub](https://economicsbydesign.com/health-system/).

Key Signals

## 5 things the data tells us

These signals emerge from analysis of UK Health Accounts, OECD statistics, and international variation.

1

### Government dominates UK health financing

**81%** of UK health spending is government-financed (£280bn of £345bn). This is high by international standards, high-income countries average ~60%. It reflects the NHS model: tax-funded, free at point of use. The government share has held broadly stable, around 81%.

2

### Out-of-pocket spending is rising

UK out-of-pocket expenditure reached **£48.5bn (14.1%)** in 2025, covering prescriptions, dental care, and private treatments. (ONS revised its out-of-pocket methodology in the 30 April 2025 release, re-estimating GP and dental expenditure, so previously published nominal figures are not directly comparable.)

3

### UK spends less of GDP than peers

At **11.4% of GDP** on current health expenditure (ONS 2025 provisional), the UK ranks mid-table among high-income countries. The US spends 17.2%, Germany 12.3%, France 11.5% (OECD HaG 2025). On the consistent OECD basis the UK figure is 11.1%; among G7 nations only Japan (10.6%) and Italy (8.4%) spend a smaller share on that basis.

4

### Curative care dominates, prevention is small

Around **two-thirds** of UK government health spending goes to curative and rehabilitative care (67% in 2024: £179.8bn of £269.1bn). Prevention spending nearly quadrupled during COVID-19 but fell back to just **5%** (£12.2bn) by 2024. See Chart 7 →

5

### Five forces drive spending growth

Population growth, ageing demographics, rising disease burden (NCDs), medical technology advances, and workforce costs all push spending upward. Without productivity gains, this trajectory is **structurally challenging**.

**⚠️ The sustainability question:** UK government health spending dipped after its 2021 COVID peak — down 3.2% in real terms by 2024 as COVID-era prevention spending unwound — yet demand continues to grow. The gap between what the system needs and what it receives is widening.

📖 Key terms explained

**ICB (Integrated Care Board):** local NHS organisations that plan and buy healthcare services for their area. They replaced CCGs in 2022; there were 42 in 2024/25, reduced to 36 by mergers from April 2026.

**NHSE (NHS England):** The arm's-length body that oversees the NHS, sets standards, and directly commissions specialised services.

**CHC (Continuing Healthcare):** Free care outside hospital for people with significant ongoing health needs.

**AHP (Allied Health Professional):** 14 registered professions including physiotherapists, occupational therapists, radiographers, and paramedics.

## Financing sources vary by country income level

How a country pays for health, not just how much, shapes who gets care and who pays at the door. The income gradient is stark. Government schemes (general taxation and compulsory social insurance pooled together) fund roughly 65% of health spending in high-income countries, falling to 56% in upper-middle, 38% in lower-middle, and just 19% in low-income. Out-of-pocket payments move the other way: 13% in high-income, peaking at 47% in lower-middle and 46% in low-income, where most household health spending is a direct cash transaction at the point of need, often catastrophic for the family bearing it. The lowest-income systems are also partly financed from outside the country: external development assistance covers around 31% of total health spending in low-income countries, against effectively zero in high-income.

The view below is the World Bank WDI four-category breakdown, which treats “Government” as a single block. That hides an important sub-story inside high-income countries, where systems split between tax-funded and social-insurance models — picked up in the annotation below the chart. The transition from OOP-heavy to pooled financing is central to [universal health coverage (opens in new tab)](https://www.who.int/health-topics/universal-health-coverage). Why It's Growing

## Five drivers of health spending growth

Health spending growth isn't policy failure, it's demographic and technological reality. These five structural forces affect every health system, regardless of how it's organised or funded. Underlying them all is rising national income: richer societies consistently choose to spend a larger share of their prosperity on health, and empirical decompositions typically find income growth and technology the largest contributors, with ageing more modest than commonly assumed.

👥

**Population growth**  
More people = more healthcare needed. Global population projected to reach 9.7bn by 2050.

👴

**Demographic ageing**  
Healthcare costs peak at birth, pregnancy, and end of life. Ageing increases high-cost phases.

💊

**Non-communicable diseases**  
NCDs (heart disease, diabetes, cancer) are rising globally and require long-term management.

🔬

**Medical technology**  
New diagnostics, treatments, and drugs extend what's treatable, but often at higher cost.

👩‍⚕️

**Workforce costs**  
Healthcare is labour-intensive. Wage growth and shortages push spending upward.

**The productivity challenge:** Unlike manufacturing, healthcare has limited scope for automation-driven productivity gains. This means spending tends to rise faster than GDP, a phenomenon economists call "Baumol's cost disease" (Baumol, W.J. 1967, _American Economic Review_; revisited in Baumol, W.J. 2012, _The Cost Disease: Why Computers Get Cheaper and Health Care Doesn't_, Yale University Press). The empirical pattern is robust across high-income systems, though the magnitude is contested: AI-enabled diagnostics, automation in back-office and pharmacy workflows, and digital triage may dampen the effect over the 2025–2050 horizon.

## Mental health expenditure: the funding gap

Mental ill-health costs OECD economies more than 4% of GDP, yet most countries spend well below the recommended 10% of health budgets on mental health services. The result is a treatment gap where ~67% of people who need mental health care are estimated to lack access to treatment.

## How do we invest in prevention?

If prevention delivers a **median £14:£1 return** (range local interventions median ~£4:£1; national regulatory measures substantially higher across 52 studies; Masters et al. 2017), why does the ringfenced Public Health Grant receive just 0.3% of total government spending, equivalent to roughly **0.3% of total managed expenditure** (the most decision-relevant denominator for prevention-vs-treatment trade-offs)? Understanding the mechanisms, and the barriers, is the first step to shifting the balance.

### The value case

£13,000

**opportunity cost**(Claxton et al. 2015)

The NHS empirical opportunity cost (£13,000) is roughly **~3.4×** the public-health marginal cost per QALY (£3,800) — i.e. at the margin, prevention buys a QALY for roughly a third of what the NHS gives up to fund treatment. Sources: [Martin, Lomas & Claxton (2020), _BMJ Open_ / CHE Research Paper 166 (opens in new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-036411) (public-health marginal cost per QALY); [Claxton et al. (2015) _Health Technology Assessment_ / CHE Research Paper 81 (opens in new tab)](https://doi.org/10.3310/hta19140) (NHS opportunity cost). Important: the NHS opportunity cost is not the "average cost per QALY of treatment", and the NICE willingness-to-pay threshold (£25–35k from April 2026) is a third, separate concept.

**Discount-rate framework:** figures use HM Treasury Green Book (3.5% costs and effects). Note the NICE reference case also applies 3.5% to both, while the HMT Green Book supplementary guidance on discounting sets 1.5% on health effects for long-horizon prevention, which can materially improve the apparent ratio for prevention investments with benefits decades out. Public-health marginal cost per QALY (£3,800) is from [Martin, Lomas & Claxton (2020) (opens in new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-036411), an econometric estimate of the marginal productivity of local public-health-grant spending (a supply-side figure, not a pooled ICER). NHS empirical opportunity cost (£13,000) is from [Claxton et al. (2015) (opens in new tab)](https://doi.org/10.3310/hta19140) at 2008 prices, representing the displaced marginal QALY (not the "average treatment cost"). The NICE willingness-to-pay threshold (£25,000–£35,000 per QALY from April 2026, uplifted from £20,000–£30,000) is a third, distinct concept and not directly comparable.

### Why doesn't it happen?

⏱️

**Short-term funding cycles**
Public health grant announced with weeks' notice. Prevention needs 5–10 year horizons.

📊

**No universal definition**
ICBs can't baseline current prevention spend, the [Hewitt Review (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-hewitt-review-an-independent-review-of-integrated-care-systems) found developing one will take "several years".

🎯

**Performance pressure**
ICBs judged on waiting lists and financial balance. Prevention doesn't show up in next quarter's metrics.

💰

**Treasury wants "cashable savings"**
Even with strong business cases, finance teams resist "jam tomorrow". The Green Book supports DALYs, but practice lags.

### What's changing

*   **[10 Year Health Plan (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/10-year-health-plan-for-england-fit-for-the-future)**: commits to "prevention accelerators" in selected ICBs, with focus on CVD and diabetes
*   **[Hewitt Review (2023) (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-hewitt-review-an-independent-review-of-integrated-care-systems) implementation**, DHSC and NHSE developing a prevention spend definition for baselining, as the Review recommended
*   **Recommendation**: increase NHS prevention spend by at least 1% of ICB budgets over 5 years (ideally 10–20% long-term)
*   **Shift from hospital to home**, Better Care Fund and DFG supporting housing-based prevention

## The bottom line

We asked: **how is health spending structured, and why does it keep growing?**

Structure

81%

gov funded

### Three channels, different equity implications

**Government transfers** dominate in the UK at 81%, among the highest globally. This is the NHS model: tax-funded, free at point of use, risk pooled across the population.

**Social insurance** (Germany, France) achieves similar coverage through employer/employee contributions but with higher administrative complexity.

**Out-of-pocket** exceeds 40% in many LMICs, creating real barriers. The UK's 14.1% OOP is a genuine strength, reducing it further is central to universal coverage globally.

Growth

+1.5%

of GDP by 2045

### Structural forces, not policy failure

Five forces drive spending upward everywhere: **population growth**, **demographic ageing**, **chronic disease burden**, **medical technology**: and **workforce costs** that outpace productivity.

Healthcare can't easily automate, a phenomenon economists call "Baumol's cost disease." OECD's central projection has public spending on health rising by a further **+1.5% of GDP by 2045** across OECD countries (OECD, _Health at a Glance 2025_); the exact pace depends on demographic, productivity, and technology assumptions.

The question isn't _whether_ to spend more. It's whether that spending translates into proportionate health gains.

Value

0.3%

prevention

### More spending ≠ better outcomes

The US spends 17.2% of GDP yet has the **lowest life expectancy** among peers (78.4 years). Japan spends 10.6% and has the highest (84.1 years). The relationship isn't linear.

What matters is _how_ money is spent. The ringfenced Public Health Grant is just **0.3% of total government spending**, cut 26% per person in real terms since 2015/16, despite a [median £14:£1 return (opens in new tab)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5537512/) across public health interventions (Masters et al. 2017).

We're treating illness, not preventing it. Every prevention business case has to overcome this structural bias toward acute care.

The real question isn't

"How much should we spend?"

It's

"How do we turn spending into health?"

### For practitioners

If you're making investment decisions in the NHS or advising on health system reform, three priorities emerge:

*   **Focus on value, not volume**: build cases around efficiency and evidence-based allocation, not just more spending
*   **Protect pooled financing**: rising OOP erodes equity; the NHS model has genuine strengths worth defending
*   **Make the case for prevention**: the ROI is there, but you'll need frameworks like the [Green Book (opens in new tab)](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-green-book-appraisal-and-evaluation-in-central-government) to overcome institutional bias

## Health expenditure: key questions answered

How much does the UK spend on healthcare?

The UK spent £345bn on healthcare in 2025 (provisional), equivalent to 11.4% of GDP on current health expenditure — the internationally comparable measure. Source: ONS UK Health Accounts 2025, OECD Health at a Glance 2025.

How does UK health spending vary internationally?

The UK ranks mid-table among high-income countries. The US spends 17.2% of GDP, Germany 12.3%, France 11.5%, the UK 11.4% (ONS 2025 provisional; 11.1% on the OECD basis), and Japan 10.6%. Among G7 nations, only Japan and Italy (8.4%) spend a smaller share on the consistent OECD basis. Source: OECD Health at a Glance 2025; ONS UK Health Accounts 2025.

What percentage of GDP does the UK spend on health?

11.4% of GDP on current health expenditure (2025 provisional). High-income countries range from around 8% to 17% of GDP, with most between 9% and 13%. Source: ONS UK Health Accounts, OECD Health at a Glance 2025.

Who pays for healthcare in the UK?

Government funds 81% of UK health spending (£280bn of £345bn), high by international standards where high-income countries average around 60%. Out-of-pocket expenditure accounts for 14.1% (£48.5bn), covering prescriptions, dental care, and private treatments. Voluntary health insurance has been the fastest-growing component (up 13.8% in real terms in 2024). Source: ONS UK Health Accounts 2025.

How much does the UK spend on public health and prevention?

Three measures with different numerators, denominators and vintages, so they are not directly comparable: **5%** of UK government health spending on the narrow ONS preventive-care category (£12.2bn of £269.1bn in 2024, ONS); **5.6%** of total current health expenditure on the broader OECD HC.6 preventive-care definition (a wider numerator covering health-protection, disease-prevention, health-promotion and surveillance); and the ringfenced Public Health Grant at just **0.3%** of total government spending (all departments). Prevention spending nearly quadrupled during COVID-19 but has since fallen back, partly a classification artefact (pandemic response was recorded as preventive care). Evidence suggests a median £14:£1 return across public health interventions (local-intervention median is £4:£1, the more decision-relevant figure for ICBs). Source: ONS UK Health Accounts 2025, OECD Health at a Glance 2025, Masters et al. 2017.

What is driving health spending growth?

Five structural forces drive health spending growth globally: population growth (9.7bn projected by 2050), demographic ageing (healthcare costs peak at end of life), rising non-communicable diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer), medical technology advances (new treatments at higher cost), and workforce costs (healthcare is labour-intensive). Public spending on health is projected to rise by a further +1.5% of GDP by 2045 on OECD's central projection. Source: OECD, Health at a Glance 2025.

How much do countries spend on mental health?

Most OECD countries spend well below the recommended 10% of health budgets on mental health. France leads at 15%, and only five countries — the UK, Canada, Germany, Norway and France — reported spending above 10% in the OECD's 2021 benchmarking (the UK value is England data). On the narrower NHS measure, the UK allocates around 8.78% of ICB baseline funding to mental health (2024/25). Mental ill-health costs OECD economies more than 4% of GDP, in the UK alone, the societal cost is estimated at £118bn per year. Source: OECD A New Benchmark for Mental Health Systems (2021, CC BY 4.0), NHS MH Dashboard, LSE/MHF (2022).

Health expenditure per capita
Copy link to Health expenditure per capita

The level of per capita health spending – which captures both individual and population healthcare needs – and how this changes over time depends on a wide range of demographic, social and economic factors, as well as the financing and organisational arrangements of a country’s health system.

In 2024, average health spending in OECD countries was estimated to stand at nearly USD 6 000 per capita (when adjusted for differences in purchasing power). The United States was the highest spender – reaching the equivalent of over USD 14 880 per person, or 2.5 times the OECD average (Figure 7.4). Switzerland, Norway and Germany followed, with per capita health spending of around two‑thirds of the level of the United States (USD 9 300‑10 000). After that, a further group of Western European countries, as well as Australia and Canada, all spent between USD 7 000 and USD 8 500 per person. Spending levels broadly decreased across Southern, Central and Eastern European countries to the Latin American OECD Member countries, with spending in Mexico (USD 1 590) at around a quarter of the OECD average. Health spending in accession/partner countries Indonesia and India was less than USD 500 per capita.

Figure 7.4 also shows the split of health spending based on the type of healthcare coverage, either organised through government health schemes or compulsory insurance, or through voluntary arrangements such as private voluntary health insurance or direct payments by households (see section “Health expenditure by financing schemes”). On average, about three‑quarters of all health spending is financed through government or compulsory insurance schemes across OECD countries.

In the years leading up to the COVID‑19 pandemic, annual per capita spending on healthcare grew by an average of 2.7% across OECD countries (Figure 7.5). In the Baltic countries, Korea and Poland, average annual spending growth during 2014‑2019 was between 5% and 8%, while in France, Italy, Finland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands annual increases were much more moderate at less than 1% on average.

Between 2019 and 2024, average annual per capita spending growth in OECD countries took place at a similar rate (2.5%) than during the pre‑pandemic period, but with substantial year-on-year differences. Across the OECD, annual growth in real terms was 5% in 2020 and peaked at 8% in 2021 as governments mobilised funds to slow down and tackle the effects of the COVID‑19 pandemic. With countries transitioning out of this health emergency, health spending contracted by around 2.5% on average in OECD countries in 2022. It stagnated in 2023 before returning to robust growth at above 3% per capita in 2024 (Figure 7.2). Some of the recent trajectory can be explained by economic and geo-political challenges that affected countries’ ability to fund any additional spending on health in 2022 and 2023, as well as high inflation rates that were often eroding nominal spending increases (Mueller, Penn and Morgan, 2024[1]).

Trends in health spending growth diverged markedly across countries and regions between 2019‑2024 as the impact of the COVID‑19 pandemic and the cost-of-living and energy crises differed between health systems. In Japan and Denmark, for example, the real level of health spending per capita stagnated when comparing 2019 and 2024. While both countries recorded high spending growth in 2021 (8%), this was followed by a subsequent drop of a similar magnitude in the subsequent year(s), resulting in a compound zero growth rate. On the other hand, Türkiye and Poland saw particularly high increases in health spending between 2019 and 2024, with average annual real growth of 8‑10%. Slovenia, the Slovak Republic and Chile also recorded robust growth during this period, at around 4‑5% on average. Latvia followed a very particular spending trajectory – with an astounding real-term spending increase of 30% in 2021, followed by substantial cuts in the two subsequent years, resulting in a compound annual growth rate close to 3%. In contrast, many countries in Western and Northern Europe, such as France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Sweden, saw only modest annual spending growth at around 1% on average – similar to or below pre‑pandemic period growth.

Definition and comparability
Copy link to Definition and comparability

See section “Health expenditure in relation to GDP” for a definition of current expenditure on health.

To compare spending levels between countries, per capita health expenditures are converted to a common currency (USD) and adjusted to take account of the difference in purchasing power of the national currencies. AIC Purchasing Power Parities (PPPs) are used as the most available and reliable conversion rates. For the calculation of growth rates in real terms, AIC deflators are used for all countries, where available.

Note that data for 2024 are based on provisional figures submitted by the country or estimated by the OECD Secretariat.

Health expenditure per capita
Copy link to Health expenditure per capita

The level of per capita health spending – which captures both individual and population healthcare needs – and how this changes over time depends on a wide range of demographic, social and economic factors, as well as the financing and organisational arrangements of a country’s health system.

In 2024, average health spending in OECD countries was estimated to stand at nearly USD 6 000 per capita (when adjusted for differences in purchasing power). The United States was the highest spender – reaching the equivalent of over USD 14 880 per person, or 2.5 times the OECD average (Figure 7.4). Switzerland, Norway and Germany followed, with per capita health spending of around two‑thirds of the level of the United States (USD 9 300‑10 000). After that, a further group of Western European countries, as well as Australia and Canada, all spent between USD 7 000 and USD 8 500 per person. Spending levels broadly decreased across Southern, Central and Eastern European countries to the Latin American OECD Member countries, with spending in Mexico (USD 1 590) at around a quarter of the OECD average. Health spending in accession/partner countries Indonesia and India was less than USD 500 per capita.

Figure 7.4 also shows the split of health spending based on the type of healthcare coverage, either organised through government health schemes or compulsory insurance, or through voluntary arrangements such as private voluntary health insurance or direct payments by households (see section “Health expenditure by financing schemes”). On average, about three‑quarters of all health spending is financed through government or compulsory insurance schemes across OECD countries.

In the years leading up to the COVID‑19 pandemic, annual per capita spending on healthcare grew by an average of 2.7% across OECD countries (Figure 7.5). In the Baltic countries, Korea and Poland, average annual spending growth during 2014‑2019 was between 5% and 8%, while in France, Italy, Finland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands annual increases were much more moderate at less than 1% on average.

Between 2019 and 2024, average annual per capita spending growth in OECD countries took place at a similar rate (2.5%) than during the pre‑pandemic period, but with substantial year-on-year differences. Across the OECD, annual growth in real terms was 5% in 2020 and peaked at 8% in 2021 as governments mobilised funds to slow down and tackle the effects of the COVID‑19 pandemic. With countries transitioning out of this health emergency, health spending contracted by around 2.5% on average in OECD countries in 2022. It stagnated in 2023 before returning to robust growth at above 3% per capita in 2024 (Figure 7.2). Some of the recent trajectory can be explained by economic and geo-political challenges that affected countries’ ability to fund any additional spending on health in 2022 and 2023, as well as high inflation rates that were often eroding nominal spending increases (Mueller, Penn and Morgan, 2024[1]).

Trends in health spending growth diverged markedly across countries and regions between 2019‑2024 as the impact of the COVID‑19 pandemic and the cost-of-living and energy crises differed between health systems. In Japan and Denmark, for example, the real level of health spending per capita stagnated when comparing 2019 and 2024. While both countries recorded high spending growth in 2021 (8%), this was followed by a subsequent drop of a similar magnitude in the subsequent year(s), resulting in a compound zero growth rate. On the other hand, Türkiye and Poland saw particularly high increases in health spending between 2019 and 2024, with average annual real growth of 8‑10%. Slovenia, the Slovak Republic and Chile also recorded robust growth during this period, at around 4‑5% on average. Latvia followed a very particular spending trajectory – with an astounding real-term spending increase of 30% in 2021, followed by substantial cuts in the two subsequent years, resulting in a compound annual growth rate close to 3%. In contrast, many countries in Western and Northern Europe, such as France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Sweden, saw only modest annual spending growth at around 1% on average – similar to or below pre‑pandemic period growth.

Definition and comparability
Copy link to Definition and comparability

See section “Health expenditure in relation to GDP” for a definition of current expenditure on health.

To compare spending levels between countries, per capita health expenditures are converted to a common currency (USD) and adjusted to take account of the difference in purchasing power of the national currencies. AIC Purchasing Power Parities (PPPs) are used as the most available and reliable conversion rates. For the calculation of growth rates in real terms, AIC deflators are used for all countries, where available.

Note that data for 2024 are based on provisional figures submitted by the country or estimated by the OECD Secretariat.

# Global Health Expenditure Database

![Image 2: Search](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Images/Navigation/search.png)[![Image 3: Home](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Images/Navigation/home_on_time.GIF)](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Home/Index/en)[Data Explorer](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Select/Indicators/en)[Visualisations](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/QuickReports/Index/en)[Documentation Centre](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/DocumentationCentre/Index/en)[Help](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Help/Index/en)[Search](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Search/Index/en)

![Image 4: SCI_cp_US](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Images/GHED_blurb_2025.jpg) The Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED) provides comparable data on health expenditure for 195 countries and territories since 2000 with open access to the public.   
  
 Health spending indicators are key guides for monitoring the flow of resources, informing health policy development, and promoting the transparency and accountability of health systems. The database can help to answer questions, such as how much countries and territories spend on health, how much of the health spending comes from government, households, and donors, and how much of the spending is channelled through compulsory and voluntary health financing arrangements. The database also includes a detailed breakdown of spending for an increasing number of countries and territories on health care functions and primary health care, spending by diseases and conditions, spending for the under 5-year-old population, and spending by provider type. Information on health capital investments is also included.   
  
 WHO works collaboratively with Member States to update the database ([Explore the Data](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Select/Indicators/en)) annually, using available information such as health accounts data, government expenditure records and official statistics. Where necessary, estimates are used to ensure the comprehensiveness and consistency of the data across countries/territories and years. In this year's GHED update, health spending in 2023 is made available. GHED is the source of the health expenditure data republished by the World Bank World Development Indicators and the WHO Global Health Observatory.   
  
 Alongside the data, the updated [visualizations of health spending](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/QuickReports/Index/en) are also online. In this section, you will be able to view individual country health expenditure profiles and PHC expenditure country profiles. In the [documentation center](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/DocumentationCentre/Index/en), you will find the December 2025 country release note, as well as complementary technical notes, methodology guidelines, health accounts training materials, global, regional, and country reports on health expenditure, etc.   
  
 As the program’s lead technical agency, WHO is committed to working closely with partners to support countries in tracking health spending and sustaining the Global Health Expenditure Database as global public goods.   
  
 For any queries, please contact: [nha@who.int](mailto:nha@who.int)

![Image 2: Search](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Images/Navigation/search.png)[![Image 3: Home](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Images/Navigation/home_on_time.GIF)](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Home/Index/en)[Data Explorer](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Select/Indicators/en)[Visualisations](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/QuickReports/Index/en)[Documentation Centre](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/DocumentationCentre/Index/en)[Help](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Help/Index/en)[Search](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Search/Index/en)

![Image 4: SCI_cp_US](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Images/GHED_blurb_2025.jpg) The Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED) provides comparable data on health expenditure for 195 countries and territories since 2000 with open access to the public.   
  
 Health spending indicators are key guides for monitoring the flow of resources, informing health policy development, and promoting the transparency and accountability of health systems. The database can help to answer questions, such as how much countries and territories spend on health, how much of the health spending comes from government, households, and donors, and how much of the spending is channelled through compulsory and voluntary health financing arrangements. The database also includes a detailed breakdown of spending for an increasing number of countries and territories on health care functions and primary health care, spending by diseases and conditions, spending for the under 5-year-old population, and spending by provider type. Information on health capital investments is also included.   
  
 WHO works collaboratively with Member States to update the database ([Explore the Data](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Select/Indicators/en)) annually, using available information such as health accounts data, government expenditure records and official statistics. Where necessary, estimates are used to ensure the comprehensiveness and consistency of the data across countries/territories and years. In this year's GHED update, health spending in 2023 is made available. GHED is the source of the health expenditure data republished by the World Bank World Development Indicators and the WHO Global Health Observatory.   
  
 Alongside the data, the updated [visualizations of health spending](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/QuickReports/Index/en) are also online. In this section, you will be able to view individual country health expenditure profiles and PHC expenditure country profiles. In the [documentation center](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/DocumentationCentre/Index/en), you will find the December 2025 country release note, as well as complementary technical notes, methodology guidelines, health accounts training materials, global, regional, and country reports on health expenditure, etc.   
  
 As the program’s lead technical agency, WHO is committed to working closely with partners to support countries in tracking health spending and sustaining the Global Health Expenditure Database as global public goods.   
  
 For any queries, please contact: [nha@who.int](mailto:nha@who.int)

## Highlights

Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720 billion in 2023. This was equivalent to 10.0% of gross domestic product (GDP).

Among EU countries, Germany (11.7%), France (11.5%), Austria and Sweden (both 11.2%) had the highest current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in 2023.

Among EU countries, the largest expansions (in percentage terms) in current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant between 2014 and 2023 were recorded in Romania, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Czechia, Estonia and Croatia, where expenditure more than doubled.

This article presents key statistics on expenditure aspects of [healthcare](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Healthcare "Glossary:Healthcare") in the [European Union (EU)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_Union_(EU) "Glossary:European Union (EU)"). More detailed information is available – with analyses by functions, providers and financing schemes – in [a separate article](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_by_function,_provider_and_financing_scheme "Healthcare expenditure statistics by function, provider and financing scheme"). Healthcare systems are organised and financed in various ways across EU countries, but universal access to quality healthcare, at an affordable cost to both individuals and society at large, is widely regarded as a basic right in the EU.

Statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing may be used to evaluate how a healthcare system responds to the challenge of universal access to quality healthcare, through measuring financial resources available for the healthcare sector and the allocation of these resources between healthcare activities (for example, preventive and curative care) or groups of healthcare providers (for example, [hospitals](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Hospital "Glossary:Hospital") and ambulatory centres).

This article forms part of an online publication on [Health in the European Union - facts and figures](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures "Health in the European Union - facts and figures").

It should be noted that the latest data presented in this article are for 2023. Therefore, the data in this article show the situation after the COVID-19 pandemic. For this reason, particular attention should be paid when comparing 2022 and 2023 data with data for 2020 to 2021 and when comparing data for 2020 and 2021 with earlier years.

## Healthcare expenditure

**Germany, France, Austria and Sweden had the highest current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in 2023**

Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720[billion](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Billion "Glossary:Billion") in 2023. Germany had the highest level of current healthcare expenditure among EU countries, valued at €492 billion in 2023. France recorded the second highest level of current healthcare expenditure (€325 billion), followed by Italy (€179 billion) and Spain (€138 billion).

In 2023, current healthcare expenditure in the EU was equivalent to 10.0% of [gross domestic product (GDP)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP) "Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)"). Among the EU countries, Germany recorded the highest ratio, which was equivalent to 11.7% of GDP; the next highest ratios were in France (11.5%), Austria and Sweden (both 11.2%) – see Table 1. By contrast, current healthcare expenditure accounted for less than 7.0% of GDP in 4 EU countries: Luxembourg, Romania (both 5.7%), Hungary (6.4%) and Ireland (6.6%).

Relative to population size and in euro terms, current healthcare expenditure in 2023 was highest among EU countries in Luxembourg (€6 888 per inhabitant). It is interesting to note that Luxembourg had the highest ratio per inhabitant despite having the lowest ratio of healthcare expenditure to GDP, reflecting the high level of GDP in Luxembourg. A significant proportion of workers in Luxembourg are cross-border workers and live outside the country and, as non-residents, the expenditure on their healthcare is not included in Luxembourg’s health accounts while their economic activity contributes to Luxembourg’s GDP.

Following on from Luxembourg, the next highest ratios in 2023 were observed in Ireland, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Sweden, all above €5 700 per inhabitant. In turn, these were followed by Belgium, Finland and France with ratios between €4 700 and €5 500 per inhabitant. There was then a relatively large gap to Malta, Italy, Spain, Slovenia, Cyprus, Portugal and Czechia with ratios above €2 400 but below €3 300 per inhabitant. All of the remaining 10 EU countries recorded average expenditure below €2 100 per inhabitant; 1 of these, Romania, recorded an average spend on healthcare below €1 000 per inhabitant. The ratio between the highest (Luxembourg) and lowest (Romania) levels of expenditure per inhabitant was 7.1:1.

The disparities in current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant are less apparent when expenditure is expressed in [purchasing power standards (PPS)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS) "Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)"). This measure adjusts for differences in price levels between EU countries. Germany (5 413 PPS per inhabitant), Austria (4 900 PPS per inhabitant) and the Netherlands (4 848 PPS per inhabitant) recorded the highest ratios of healthcare expenditure per inhabitant in PPS terms. Romania (1 776 PPS per inhabitant) had the lowest ratio. As such, by taking account of price level differences, the ratio between the highest (Germany) and lowest (Romania) levels of healthcare expenditure per inhabitant was considerably smaller than the equivalent ratio in euro terms mentioned above, as it was 3.0:1.

## Developments over time

Table 2 and Figures 2 and 3 highlight developments in the level of healthcare expenditure and the level of healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in recent years, focusing on a comparison between 2014 and 2023. Note that the analyses in Table 2 and Figure 2 are presented in current price terms and so reflect price changes (inflation and deflation) as well as changes in real expenditure.

Based on the data shown in Table 2, all EU countries recorded higher healthcare expenditure in 2023 than in 2014. The largest overall increases were observed in Romania, Lithuania, Malta, Bulgaria, Estonia, Czechia, Latvia, Cyprus and Poland, where expenditure in 2023 was more than double that in 2014. The highest increase, in Romania, was 144.7%, equivalent to a compound annual average increase of 10.5%. The smallest increases between 2014 and 2023 were observed in Italy (up 23.6% overall) and Sweden (25.1%).

**Current healthcare expenditure**

Current healthcare expenditure quantifies the economic resources dedicated to health functions, excluding capital investment. Current healthcare expenditure is primarily concerned with healthcare goods and services that are consumed by resident units, irrespective of where that consumption takes place (it may be in the rest of the world) or who is paying for it. As such, exports of healthcare goods and services (to non-resident units) are excluded, whereas imports of healthcare goods and services for final use are included.

**System of health accounts – methodology**

[Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Eurostat "Glossary:Eurostat"), the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD) "Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)") and the [World Health Organization (WHO)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:World_Health_Organization_(WHO) "Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)") established a common framework for a joint healthcare data collection exercise. The data collected relates to healthcare expenditure following the methodology of the [system of health accounts (SHA)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:System_of_health_accounts_(SHA) "Glossary:System of health accounts (SHA)").

The SHA shares the goals of the [system of national accounts (SNA)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:System_of_national_accounts_(SNA) "Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)"): to constitute an integrated system of comprehensive, internally consistent and internationally comparable accounts, which should as far as possible be compatible with other aggregated economic and social statistical systems. Health accounts provide a description of the monetary flows related to final consumption expenditure on healthcare goods and services. Health accounts are used in 2 main ways: internationally, where the emphasis is on a selection of comparable expenditure data; nationally, with more detailed analyses of healthcare spending and a greater emphasis on comparisons over time.

For more details on health accounts, see [A system of health accounts, 2011 – revised edition](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf/60aa44b0-2738-4c4d-be4b-48b6590be1b0). The core set of SHA tables addresses 3 basic questions: i) what kinds of healthcare goods and services are consumed, ii) which healthcare providers deliver them and, iii) which financing schemes are used to finance the expenditure?

**Healthcare expenditure – legal basis**

[Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1901 of 29 October 2021 as regards statistics on health care expenditure and financing](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.387.01.0110.01.ENG) is the legal basis for data collection according to SHA 2011 methodology for healthcare expenditure. [Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/359 of 4 March 2015 implementing Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008 as regards statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32015R0359:EN:NOT) applied to data from reference year 2014 to 2020.

Statistics on healthcare expenditure are documented in a [background article](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_-_methodology "Healthcare expenditure statistics - methodology") which provides more information on the scope of the data, the legal framework, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions.

## Context

Health systems across the globe are developing in response to a multitude of factors, including new medical technology and improvements in knowledge providing new health services and a greater access to them; changes in health policies to address specific diseases and demographic developments; new organisational structures and more complex financing mechanisms. However, access to healthcare and greater patient choice is increasingly being considered against a background of financial sustainability.

Within the European Commission, the [Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety](https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/health-and-food-safety_en) and the [Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion](https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/employment-social-affairs-and-inclusion_en) are responsible for policy actions on health.

_[Regulation (EU)2021/522 establishing a Programme for the Union’s action in the field of health (‘EU4health programme’) for the period 2021 to 2027](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L\_.2021.107.01.0001.01.ENG)_ provides funding to EU countries, health organisations and non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

In May 2024, the European Commission summarised work done and progress made within the health domain through a communication _[The European Health Union: acting together for people’s health](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0206)_ (COM(2024)206 final). It highlights a range of actions designed to make people’s lives safer and healthier.

The Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety has constituted a list of 88 [European core health indicators (ECHIs)](https://health.ec.europa.eu/indicators-and-data/european-core-health-indicators-echi_en) for monitoring progress in relation to health policy and broader objectives. Among these, it specifically recommends following developments on:

*   [expenditure on healthcare as a percentage of GDP](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77a)
*   [expenditures on healthcare in purchasing power standards (PPS)](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77b).

## Highlights

Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720 billion in 2023. This was equivalent to 10.0% of gross domestic product (GDP).

Among EU countries, Germany (11.7%), France (11.5%), Austria and Sweden (both 11.2%) had the highest current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in 2023.

Among EU countries, the largest expansions (in percentage terms) in current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant between 2014 and 2023 were recorded in Romania, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Czechia, Estonia and Croatia, where expenditure more than doubled.

This article presents key statistics on expenditure aspects of [healthcare](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Healthcare "Glossary:Healthcare") in the [European Union (EU)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_Union_(EU) "Glossary:European Union (EU)"). More detailed information is available – with analyses by functions, providers and financing schemes – in [a separate article](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_by_function,_provider_and_financing_scheme "Healthcare expenditure statistics by function, provider and financing scheme"). Healthcare systems are organised and financed in various ways across EU countries, but universal access to quality healthcare, at an affordable cost to both individuals and society at large, is widely regarded as a basic right in the EU.

Statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing may be used to evaluate how a healthcare system responds to the challenge of universal access to quality healthcare, through measuring financial resources available for the healthcare sector and the allocation of these resources between healthcare activities (for example, preventive and curative care) or groups of healthcare providers (for example, [hospitals](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Hospital "Glossary:Hospital") and ambulatory centres).

This article forms part of an online publication on [Health in the European Union - facts and figures](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures "Health in the European Union - facts and figures").

It should be noted that the latest data presented in this article are for 2023. Therefore, the data in this article show the situation after the COVID-19 pandemic. For this reason, particular attention should be paid when comparing 2022 and 2023 data with data for 2020 to 2021 and when comparing data for 2020 and 2021 with earlier years.

## Healthcare expenditure

**Germany, France, Austria and Sweden had the highest current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in 2023**

Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720[billion](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Billion "Glossary:Billion") in 2023. Germany had the highest level of current healthcare expenditure among EU countries, valued at €492 billion in 2023. France recorded the second highest level of current healthcare expenditure (€325 billion), followed by Italy (€179 billion) and Spain (€138 billion).

In 2023, current healthcare expenditure in the EU was equivalent to 10.0% of [gross domestic product (GDP)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP) "Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)"). Among the EU countries, Germany recorded the highest ratio, which was equivalent to 11.7% of GDP; the next highest ratios were in France (11.5%), Austria and Sweden (both 11.2%) – see Table 1. By contrast, current healthcare expenditure accounted for less than 7.0% of GDP in 4 EU countries: Luxembourg, Romania (both 5.7%), Hungary (6.4%) and Ireland (6.6%).

Relative to population size and in euro terms, current healthcare expenditure in 2023 was highest among EU countries in Luxembourg (€6 888 per inhabitant). It is interesting to note that Luxembourg had the highest ratio per inhabitant despite having the lowest ratio of healthcare expenditure to GDP, reflecting the high level of GDP in Luxembourg. A significant proportion of workers in Luxembourg are cross-border workers and live outside the country and, as non-residents, the expenditure on their healthcare is not included in Luxembourg’s health accounts while their economic activity contributes to Luxembourg’s GDP.

Following on from Luxembourg, the next highest ratios in 2023 were observed in Ireland, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Sweden, all above €5 700 per inhabitant. In turn, these were followed by Belgium, Finland and France with ratios between €4 700 and €5 500 per inhabitant. There was then a relatively large gap to Malta, Italy, Spain, Slovenia, Cyprus, Portugal and Czechia with ratios above €2 400 but below €3 300 per inhabitant. All of the remaining 10 EU countries recorded average expenditure below €2 100 per inhabitant; 1 of these, Romania, recorded an average spend on healthcare below €1 000 per inhabitant. The ratio between the highest (Luxembourg) and lowest (Romania) levels of expenditure per inhabitant was 7.1:1.

The disparities in current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant are less apparent when expenditure is expressed in [purchasing power standards (PPS)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS) "Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)"). This measure adjusts for differences in price levels between EU countries. Germany (5 413 PPS per inhabitant), Austria (4 900 PPS per inhabitant) and the Netherlands (4 848 PPS per inhabitant) recorded the highest ratios of healthcare expenditure per inhabitant in PPS terms. Romania (1 776 PPS per inhabitant) had the lowest ratio. As such, by taking account of price level differences, the ratio between the highest (Germany) and lowest (Romania) levels of healthcare expenditure per inhabitant was considerably smaller than the equivalent ratio in euro terms mentioned above, as it was 3.0:1.

## Developments over time

Table 2 and Figures 2 and 3 highlight developments in the level of healthcare expenditure and the level of healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in recent years, focusing on a comparison between 2014 and 2023. Note that the analyses in Table 2 and Figure 2 are presented in current price terms and so reflect price changes (inflation and deflation) as well as changes in real expenditure.

Based on the data shown in Table 2, all EU countries recorded higher healthcare expenditure in 2023 than in 2014. The largest overall increases were observed in Romania, Lithuania, Malta, Bulgaria, Estonia, Czechia, Latvia, Cyprus and Poland, where expenditure in 2023 was more than double that in 2014. The highest increase, in Romania, was 144.7%, equivalent to a compound annual average increase of 10.5%. The smallest increases between 2014 and 2023 were observed in Italy (up 23.6% overall) and Sweden (25.1%).

As well as being affected by price changes, comparisons of healthcare expenditure over time can also be influenced by demographic changes. Figure 2 shows the average healthcare expenditure per inhabitant in 2014 and 2023. All EU countries recorded a higher level of expenditure per inhabitant in 2023 than in 2014. As with the rate of change based on overall expenditure, Romania recorded the largest increase, with average expenditure per inhabitant increasing by 155.6%; in Bulgaria, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Czechia, Estonia and Croatia, this ratio also at least doubled. The smallest increase was observed in Sweden, up 15.2%.

Figure 3 provides another analysis of the change in overall healthcare expenditure between 2014 and 2023, focusing on the ratio between this expenditure and GDP. Healthcare expenditure and GDP are both influenced by price changes and so, when combining the 2 indicators in a ratio, the impact of inflation may cancel out to some degree: this depends on the extent to which the price changes related to healthcare expenditure are similar to those experienced in the economy as a whole.

There were 7 EU countries that reported a lower ratio of healthcare expenditure to GDP in 2023 than in 2014. Ireland recorded the largest decrease, down 2.7 [percentage points](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Percentage_point "Glossary:Percentage point"), its share falling from 9.2% in 2014 to 6.6% in 2023, in part reflecting a large increase in Irish GDP between these years. The 6 other decreases were smaller than 1.0 points. In EU countries where the ratio was higher in 2023 than it had been in 2014, the increase was not more than 1.2 percentage points in most cases. A larger increase was observed in Latvia, up 1.6 points.

**Current healthcare expenditure**

Current healthcare expenditure quantifies the economic resources dedicated to health functions, excluding capital investment. Current healthcare expenditure is primarily concerned with healthcare goods and services that are consumed by resident units, irrespective of where that consumption takes place (it may be in the rest of the world) or who is paying for it. As such, exports of healthcare goods and services (to non-resident units) are excluded, whereas imports of healthcare goods and services for final use are included.

**System of health accounts – methodology**

[Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Eurostat "Glossary:Eurostat"), the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD) "Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)") and the [World Health Organization (WHO)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:World_Health_Organization_(WHO) "Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)") established a common framework for a joint healthcare data collection exercise. The data collected relates to healthcare expenditure following the methodology of the [system of health accounts (SHA)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:System_of_health_accounts_(SHA) "Glossary:System of health accounts (SHA)").

The SHA shares the goals of the [system of national accounts (SNA)](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:System_of_national_accounts_(SNA) "Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)"): to constitute an integrated system of comprehensive, internally consistent and internationally comparable accounts, which should as far as possible be compatible with other aggregated economic and social statistical systems. Health accounts provide a description of the monetary flows related to final consumption expenditure on healthcare goods and services. Health accounts are used in 2 main ways: internationally, where the emphasis is on a selection of comparable expenditure data; nationally, with more detailed analyses of healthcare spending and a greater emphasis on comparisons over time.

For more details on health accounts, see [A system of health accounts, 2011 – revised edition](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf/60aa44b0-2738-4c4d-be4b-48b6590be1b0). The core set of SHA tables addresses 3 basic questions: i) what kinds of healthcare goods and services are consumed, ii) which healthcare providers deliver them and, iii) which financing schemes are used to finance the expenditure?

**Healthcare expenditure – legal basis**

[Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1901 of 29 October 2021 as regards statistics on health care expenditure and financing](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.387.01.0110.01.ENG) is the legal basis for data collection according to SHA 2011 methodology for healthcare expenditure. [Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/359 of 4 March 2015 implementing Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008 as regards statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing](http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32015R0359:EN:NOT) applied to data from reference year 2014 to 2020.

Statistics on healthcare expenditure are documented in a [background article](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_-_methodology "Healthcare expenditure statistics - methodology") which provides more information on the scope of the data, the legal framework, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions.

## Context

Health systems across the globe are developing in response to a multitude of factors, including new medical technology and improvements in knowledge providing new health services and a greater access to them; changes in health policies to address specific diseases and demographic developments; new organisational structures and more complex financing mechanisms. However, access to healthcare and greater patient choice is increasingly being considered against a background of financial sustainability.

Within the European Commission, the [Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety](https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/health-and-food-safety_en) and the [Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion](https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/employment-social-affairs-and-inclusion_en) are responsible for policy actions on health.

_[Regulation (EU)2021/522 establishing a Programme for the Union’s action in the field of health (‘EU4health programme’) for the period 2021 to 2027](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L\_.2021.107.01.0001.01.ENG)_ provides funding to EU countries, health organisations and non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

In May 2024, the European Commission summarised work done and progress made within the health domain through a communication _[The European Health Union: acting together for people’s health](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0206)_ (COM(2024)206 final). It highlights a range of actions designed to make people’s lives safer and healthier.

The Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety has constituted a list of 88 [European core health indicators (ECHIs)](https://health.ec.europa.eu/indicators-and-data/european-core-health-indicators-echi_en) for monitoring progress in relation to health policy and broader objectives. Among these, it specifically recommends following developments on:

*   [expenditure on healthcare as a percentage of GDP](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77a)
*   [expenditures on healthcare in purchasing power standards (PPS)](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77b).

# Health funding data analysis

Our analysis looks at health and social care funding in the UK, highlighting changes over time, the impact of COVID-19, variation across the UK and comparisons to other countries.

We have set out below the trends for health budgets in the UK and in England focusing on total budgets and resource budgets only.

For more detailed analysis of capital funding in England and the UK, see our [Capital funding analysis page](https://www.bma.org.uk/advice-and-support/nhs-delivery-and-workforce/funding/capital-funding-analysis "Capital funding analysis").

### Nominal terms vs real-terms budgets

Budgets can be expressed in nominal terms (the cash or ‘face’ value of the budget at the time it was announced) or in real terms (the value of the budget adjusted for inflation). This page uses the real-terms value of budgets in 2023/24 prices, using June 2024 [GDP Deflators](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/gdp-deflators-at-market-prices-and-money-gdp-march-2024-budget-2024).

 How health funding is measured 

Health spending can be measured in different ways, from government departmental budgets to health expenditure. Our analysis below uses two different measures:

*   Department of Health budgets. HM Treasury statistical data sets out annual information on government spending and provides long-term historical data on departmental budgets and the amount allocated to the DHSC (Department of Health and Social Care).
*   Health Expenditure. Beyond the spending of the DHSC, other departments do have expenditure that can be classified as health spending – such as the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology spending on health research. Departmental spending is broken down by the Treasury according to its function, including health. This allows for standardised cross-country comparators.

## Health funding in the UK

### How health budgets are allocated in the UK

Since health is a devolved matter, each UK nation has responsibility for their own healthcare budgets. Funding for the NHS in England comes from the Department of Health and Social Care. Funding for health and social care is allocated separately to other UK nations through a block grant, which provides an equivalent, population-adjusted level of funding for health and care – although each nation can choose how much they spend on the health and care system.

However, we can look at cumulative health expenditure for the whole of the UK to identify nation-wide trends in health spending and to make international comparisons.

### Health spending in the UK tends to increase every year, but so does demand for healthcare

Health expenditure – the money spent on health across all government departments – has increased significantly over the decades since the NHS was established in 1948. Even when accounting for inflation, health spending tends to increase year on year. In recent years, it has increased even more than usual due to additional COVID-19 funding.

The UK is not alone in this. Health spending has increased over the decades in nearly all comparable countries. This is due to population growth, ageing populations with increasingly complex healthcare needs, and increases in the relative costs of treatments including drug prices. When looking at real-terms health spend per person, annual real-terms growth is more modest.

### Health spending growth has been below average since 2010, resulting in a cumulative underspend of hundreds of billions

Growth in health spending has not been consistent during the past few decades, and the annual growth rate of real-terms expenditure varies significantly. However, in the decade preceding the pandemic, annual spending increases were significantly below the long-term historical average for nine subsequent years. This has resulted in a large cumulative underspend since 2009/10.

Additional COVID-19 funding during the pandemic meant that health spending reached close to where it would have been had growth in spending not fallen over the past decade. However, this additional funding does not make up for the cumulative underspend when comparing actual spend to the historical average.

### How the UK compares internationally

International comparisons in healthcare expenditure can be done in different ways. One way is to look at health expenditure as a % of GDP, which shows how much is spent on health relative to a country’s economy. Another way is to look at health expenditure per head of population, which shows how much is spent per person.

When looking at expenditure as a % of GDP, UK spending is about average. However, this is partially because GDP growth in the UK has been sluggish since the pandemic. Prior to the pandemic, healthcare spending in the UK as a percentage of GDP had historically been below many comparable countries such as France and Germany. When looking at health spend per person – and accounting for the spending power of different currencies – it is clear that the UK spends less than many comparable nations.

### Regional variation within the UK

Healthcare spending per person is uneven across the UK, and is the lowest in England. Between 2019/22 and 2021/22, additional COVID-19 funding significantly increased health spend per person in all nations, though it has fallen sharply since the end of the pandemic.

## Health funding in England

### Health budgets have been eroded by inflation

The day-to-day budget for the Department of Health and Social Care tends to increase in real terms every year. This is necessary because healthcare is increasingly expensive due to population growth, ageing populations with increasingly complex healthcare needs, and increases in the relative costs of treatments including drug prices.

However, the DHSC day-to-day budget has fallen in real terms for three consecutive years between 2021/22 and 2024/25.

What is more, these real-term budget cuts have now offset COVID spending increases. Though the pandemic triggered huge cash injections into the DHSC budget, subsequent real-terms cuts mean that spending for the coming year is now lower than where it would have been if, instead, the budget was increased by the historical average of every year since the start of this Parliament.

The vast majority of the DHSC budget goes to NHS England. The day-to-day budget for NHS England has also seen real terms cuts in recent years. Even increased spending during the pandemic does not make up for these cuts.

Though modest growth for the NHS budget is expected in 2024/25 compared to 2023/24, it is well below the long-term average growth rate for this budget and does not make up for past underspending.

This comes at a time where the NHS is struggling with the growing burden of waiting lists and an ageing population. What is needed are real-terms increases, not real-terms cuts.

What is more, if the Government wants to meet its commitments in the Long-Term Workforce Plan, more funding will be needed. The [Institute for Fiscal Studies](https://ifs.org.uk/publications/implications-nhs-workforce-plan) estimates that the plan implies annual NHS budget increases of around 3.6% per year in real terms.

### Regional variation in England

We can also look at health expenditure by region. There is significant variation between regions in England, with London having the highest healthcare spend per person, and regions in the East (East of England, South East, and the East Midlands) among the lowest in terms of spend per person. In the last two years, spending per person fell in real terms in all English regions. The removal of additional Covid-19 funding has also been felt more keenly in some places than others, with London only experiencing an 8% drop in funding since 2020-21, whereas funding to the South East has fallen by 14% in the same amount of time.

Significant differences in per-person healthcare spend can result in differences in the care people receive. However, regions with lower levels of health may receive more health funding, insofar as funding allocations for different geographical areas take the demography and health needs of the population into account. In part, this explains the geographical differences.

## What the BMA is doing

It is clear that health budgets are not growing fast enough to keep up with demand. Staff have also had to put up with sub-inflationary pay rises since 2008, leaving them feeling undervalued and burnt out.

The BMA continues to lobby the Government on this issue, for example through submitting regular representations to the Treasury in advance of fiscal events.[Submissions can be accessed on our website](https://www.bma.org.uk/what-we-do/working-with-uk-governments/governments/uk-consultations-briefings-and-legislation "UK consultations, briefings and legislation").
