# Health funding data analysis

Our analysis looks at health and social care funding in the UK, highlighting changes over time, the impact of COVID-19, variation across the UK and comparisons to other countries.

[](https://twitter.com/share?url=https://www.bma.org.uk/advice-and-support/nhs-delivery-and-workforce/funding/health-funding-data-analysis&text=Health%20funding%20data%20analysis&via=TheBMA)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.bma.org.uk/advice-and-support/nhs-delivery-and-workforce/funding/health-funding-data-analysis)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https://www.bma.org.uk/advice-and-support/nhs-delivery-and-workforce/funding/health-funding-data-analysis&title=Health%20funding%20data%20analysis)[](mailto:?subject=Health%20funding%20data%20analysis&body=Check%20out%20this%20site:%20https://www.bma.org.uk/advice-and-support/nhs-delivery-and-workforce/funding/health-funding-data-analysis)

![Image 38: NHS pressures waiting list](https://www.bma.org.uk/media/4876/nhs-pressures-waiting-list.svg?width=505&height=379&v=1d803b2745ddc80)

We have set out below the trends for health budgets in the UK and in England focusing on total budgets and resource budgets only.

For more detailed analysis of capital funding in England and the UK, see our [Capital funding analysis page](https://www.bma.org.uk/advice-and-support/nhs-delivery-and-workforce/funding/capital-funding-analysis "Capital funding analysis").

### Nominal terms vs real-terms budgets

Budgets can be expressed in nominal terms (the cash or ‘face’ value of the budget at the time it was announced) or in real terms (the value of the budget adjusted for inflation). This page uses the real-terms value of budgets in 2023/24 prices, using June 2024 [GDP Deflators](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/gdp-deflators-at-market-prices-and-money-gdp-march-2024-budget-2024).

 How health funding is measured 

Health spending can be measured in different ways, from government departmental budgets to health expenditure. Our analysis below uses two different measures:

*   Department of Health budgets. HM Treasury statistical data sets out annual information on government spending and provides long-term historical data on departmental budgets and the amount allocated to the DHSC (Department of Health and Social Care).
*   Health Expenditure. Beyond the spending of the DHSC, other departments do have expenditure that can be classified as health spending – such as the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology spending on health research. Departmental spending is broken down by the Treasury according to its function, including health. This allows for standardised cross-country comparators. 

>>Skip to: Health funding in England

## Health funding in the UK

### How health budgets are allocated in the UK

Since health is a devolved matter, each UK nation has responsibility for their own healthcare budgets. Funding for the NHS in England comes from the Department of Health and Social Care. Funding for health and social care is allocated separately to other UK nations through a block grant, which provides an equivalent, population-adjusted level of funding for health and care – although each nation can choose how much they spend on the health and care system.

However, we can look at cumulative health expenditure for the whole of the UK to identify nation-wide trends in health spending and to make international comparisons.

### Health spending in the UK tends to increase every year, but so does demand for healthcare

Health expenditure – the money spent on health across all government departments – has increased significantly over the decades since the NHS was established in 1948. Even when accounting for inflation, health spending tends to increase year on year. In recent years, it has increased even more than usual due to additional COVID-19 funding.

The UK is not alone in this. Health spending has increased over the decades in nearly all comparable countries. This is due to population growth, ageing populations with increasingly complex healthcare needs, and increases in the relative costs of treatments including drug prices. When looking at real-terms health spend per person, annual real-terms growth is more modest.

### Health spending growth has been below average since 2010, resulting in a cumulative underspend of hundreds of billions

Growth in health spending has not been consistent during the past few decades, and the annual growth rate of real-terms expenditure varies significantly. However, in the decade preceding the pandemic, annual spending increases were significantly below the long-term historical average for nine subsequent years. This has resulted in a large cumulative underspend since 2009/10.

Additional COVID-19 funding during the pandemic meant that health spending reached close to where it would have been had growth in spending not fallen over the past decade. However, this additional funding does not make up for the cumulative underspend when comparing actual spend to the historical average.

### How the UK compares internationally

International comparisons in healthcare expenditure can be done in different ways. One way is to look at health expenditure as a % of GDP, which shows how much is spent on health relative to a country’s economy. Another way is to look at health expenditure per head of population, which shows how much is spent per person.

When looking at expenditure as a % of GDP, UK spending is about average. However, this is partially because GDP growth in the UK has been sluggish since the pandemic. Prior to the pandemic, healthcare spending in the UK as a percentage of GDP had historically been below many comparable countries such as France and Germany. When looking at health spend per person – and accounting for the spending power of different currencies – it is clear that the UK spends less than many comparable nations.

### Regional variation within the UK

Healthcare spending per person is uneven across the UK, and is the lowest in England. Between 2019/22 and 2021/22, additional COVID-19 funding significantly increased health spend per person in all nations, though it has fallen sharply since the end of the pandemic.

## Health funding in England

### Health budgets have been eroded by inflation

The day-to-day budget for the Department of Health and Social Care tends to increase in real terms every year. This is necessary because healthcare is increasingly expensive due to population growth, ageing populations with increasingly complex healthcare needs, and increases in the relative costs of treatments including drug prices.

However, the DHSC day-to-day budget has fallen in real terms for three consecutive years between 2021/22 and 2024/25.

What is more, these real-term budget cuts have now offset COVID spending increases. Though the pandemic triggered huge cash injections into the DHSC budget, subsequent real-terms cuts mean that spending for the coming year is now lower than where it would have been if, instead, the budget was increased by the historical average of every year since the start of this Parliament.

The vast majority of the DHSC budget goes to NHS England. The day-to-day budget for NHS England has also seen real terms cuts in recent years. Even increased spending during the pandemic does not make up for these cuts.

Though modest growth for the NHS budget is expected in 2024/25 compared to 2023/24, it is well below the long-term average growth rate for this budget and does not make up for past underspending.

This comes at a time where the NHS is struggling with the growing burden of waiting lists and an ageing population. What is needed are real-terms increases, not real-terms cuts.

What is more, if the Government wants to meet its commitments in the Long-Term Workforce Plan, more funding will be needed. The [Institute for Fiscal Studies](https://ifs.org.uk/publications/implications-nhs-workforce-plan) estimates that the plan implies annual NHS budget increases of around 3.6% per year in real terms.

### Regional variation in England

We can also look at health expenditure by region. There is significant variation between regions in England, with London having the highest healthcare spend per person, and regions in the East (East of England, South East, and the East Midlands) among the lowest in terms of spend per person. In the last two years, spending per person fell in real terms in all English regions. The removal of additional Covid-19 funding has also been felt more keenly in some places than others, with London only experiencing an 8% drop in funding since 2020-21, whereas funding to the South East has fallen by 14% in the same amount of time.

Significant differences in per-person healthcare spend can result in differences in the care people receive. However, regions with lower levels of health may receive more health funding, insofar as funding allocations for different geographical areas take the demography and health needs of the population into account. In part, this explains the geographical differences.

## What the BMA is doing

It is clear that health budgets are not growing fast enough to keep up with demand. Staff have also had to put up with sub-inflationary pay rises since 2008, leaving them feeling undervalued and burnt out.

The BMA continues to lobby the Government on this issue, for example through submitting regular representations to the Treasury in advance of fiscal events.[Submissions can be accessed on our website](https://www.bma.org.uk/what-we-do/working-with-uk-governments/governments/uk-consultations-briefings-and-legislation "UK consultations, briefings and legislation").

# Trends in maternal mortality 2000 to 2023: estimates by WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank Group and UNDESA/Population Division

7 April 2025

|Publication

![Image 13: Trends in maternal mortality 2000 to 2023: estimates by WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank Group and UNDESA/Population Division](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/7e671f1b-a2d9-4267-954d-23e251ab4201/content)

### Overview

Every day in 2023, over 700 women died from preventable causes related to pregnancy and childbirth - meaning that approximately one woman is dying every two minutes.

Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target 3.1 is to reduce maternal mortality to less than 70 maternal deaths per 100 000 live births by 2030.

The United Nations Maternal Mortality Estimation Inter-Agency Group (MMEIG) – comprising WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the World Bank Group and the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (UNDESA/Population Division) has collaborated with external technical experts on a new round of estimates covering 2000 to 2023. The estimates represent the most up to date, internationally-comparable MMEIG estimates of maternal mortality, using refined input data and methods from previous rounds.

The report presents internationally comparable global, regional and country-level estimates and trends for maternal mortality between 2000 and 2023.

# Trends in maternal mortality 2000 to 2023: estimates by WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank Group and UNDESA/Population Division

7 April 2025

|Publication

![Image 13: Trends in maternal mortality 2000 to 2023: estimates by WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank Group and UNDESA/Population Division](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/7e671f1b-a2d9-4267-954d-23e251ab4201/content)

[Download (4.6 MB)](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/29f43a3d-2228-489c-b1e7-b2f28e9101ce/content)

### Overview

Every day in 2023, over 700 women died from preventable causes related to pregnancy and childbirth - meaning that approximately one woman is dying every two minutes.

Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target 3.1 is to reduce maternal mortality to less than 70 maternal deaths per 100 000 live births by 2030.

The United Nations Maternal Mortality Estimation Inter-Agency Group (MMEIG) – comprising WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the World Bank Group and the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (UNDESA/Population Division) has collaborated with external technical experts on a new round of estimates covering 2000 to 2023. The estimates represent the most up to date, internationally-comparable MMEIG estimates of maternal mortality, using refined input data and methods from previous rounds.

The report presents internationally comparable global, regional and country-level estimates and trends for maternal mortality between 2000 and 2023.

Abstract

Infant mortality remains unequally distributed across Latin America and the Caribbean. We examined
whether within-country changes in poverty, income inequality, education, government health expenditure,
and universal health coverage (UHC) were associated with infant mortality. We created an auditable
panel from a frozen World Bank API snapshot for 2000–2023. From 7,056 indicator-country-year records,
we constructed 1,008 country-years; the primary complete-case sample included 290 country-years from
17 countries with at least two informative observations. We estimated log-linear country and year ﬁx  ed-
effects models using country-clustered CR1 intervals, a t(16) reference distribution, restricted Webb-
weight wild cluster bootstrap-t inference, and cluster-jackknife checks. No predictor showed robust
evidence of association in the primary model. A one-point UHC increase corresponded to 1.51% lower
infant mortality (95% CI, -3.51% to 0.54%; bootstrap p = 0.316), and a one-percentage-point increase in
government health expenditure corresponded to 2.80% lower infant mortality (95% CI, -7.18% to 1.79%;
bootstrap p = 0.219). First-difference models produced stronger inverse estimates, but these post hoc
results were unstable across speciﬁcations. E  cological measurement, missingness, unbalanced
coverage, and few countries constrain inference. The ﬁndings do not establish causal or policy eff  ects.

1. Introduction

Infant mortality is a widely used sentinel of population health because deaths during the ﬁrst y  ear of life
reﬂect a combination of maternal and newborn car  e, nutrition, infectious disease control, living
conditions, and broader social protection. Regional declines have been substantial, yet national averages
continue to conceal marked inequalities across and within countries [1].

The social-determinants framework distinguishes structural conditions, such as income distribution and
poverty, from intermediate conditions, including education, access to care, and the organization and
ﬁnancing of health systems [  2]. Universal health coverage is multidimensional: service coverage and
ﬁnancial pr  otection should be monitored jointly. The service-coverage index used here is a unitless 0-100
composite calculated as the geometric mean of 14 tracer indicators; it is not a percentage of health
needs met [3, 4].

Relevant regional evidence is heterogeneous. A 2000–2019 panel analysis identiﬁed health expenditur  e,
female literacy, education expenditure, and other factors as correlates of infant mortality [5]. Municipal-
level machine-learning analyses in Brazil, Ecuador, and Mexico ranked poverty, illiteracy, and the Gini
index as important predictors of under-ﬁv  e mortality, while emphasizing non-linearity rather than causal
effects [6]. A panel study of 35 countries in the Americas reported a small and imprecise positive
association between the Gini index and neonatal mortality [7]. Stronger causal claims have generally
come from subnational evaluations of deﬁned policies, such as conditional cash-tr  ansfer programmes,
rather than from national ecological panels [8, 9]. Regional health-system reform scholarship has
likewise emphasized that equity in child health depends on governance, access, and implementation, not
spending aggregates alone [10].

The genuine contribution of this study is therefore not the ﬁrst use of panel data in the r  egion. It is the
combination of an updated 2000–2023 multi-domain panel, a frozen and hash-audited extraction
pipeline, explicit accounting for country-speciﬁc data contribution, and inf  erence designed for a small
number of unequal country clusters. These features address reproducibility and inferential weaknesses
in the supplied draft while preserving the ecological question.

The primary objective was to estimate the association between within-country changes in extreme
poverty, income inequality, government health expenditure, UHC service coverage, and lower-secondary
educational completion and contemporaneous changes in infant mortality. Directional expectations were
positive for poverty and inequality and negative for health expenditure, UHC, and education; these
hypotheses were not preregistered. The estimand is associational, not causal.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Study Design and Setting

We conducted an ecological longitudinal study with the country-year as the unit of analysis. The source
frame contained 42 countries and territories classiﬁed in the supplied r  egional ﬁle as Latin America and
the Caribbean. The observation window was 2000–2023. The analysis used a data snapshot
downloaded on 14 July 2026 and did not refresh values after the freeze.
2.2. Data Source and Auditable Pipeline

Seven indicators were retrieved from the public World Bank API and stored as raw JSON ﬁles.  The
pipeline used RAW, SILVER, and GOLD layers, retained API and source manifests, recorded data-quality
checks, and stored SHA-256 hashes. In the independent audit, all seven raw-ﬁle hashes matched the
supplied manifest and no duplicate country-year-indicator keys were detected [11].

2.4. Data Quality, Missingness, and Analytic Sample

The wide panel contained 1,008 potential country-years. Complete-case analysis required non-missing

complete country-years, yielding 290 observations from 17 countries.

The supplied draft used average indicator coverage of at least 80% as the main country-selection rule.
That rule was not retained because an average can mask near-total absence of a single predictor:
Argentina passed the rule but contributed only two complete years because the education indicator was
largely missing. A stable-history sensitivity analysis required at least ten complete years. No values were
imputed because missingness was extensive, variable-speciﬁc, and str  ongly structured by survey and
reporting schedules; the consequences of complete-case selection were evaluated through alternative
sample deﬁnitions. Because this was a ﬁx  ed secondary dataset, no prospective power calculation was
performed. Precision was constrained primarily by the 17 country clusters and their unequal
contributions; the analysis therefore emphasizes conﬁdence inter  vals and few-cluster inference rather
than a nominal power target.
2.5. Conceptual Model and Target Estimand

Poverty and inequality were treated as structural social conditions; education as a human-capital and
social-resource indicator; and government health expenditure and UHC service coverage as health-
system indicators. These variables can share causes, mediate one another, and respond to health
conditions. Country ﬁx  ed effects remove time-invariant national characteristics, and year ﬁx  ed effects
remove shocks common to all countries, but neither addresses unmeasured time-varying confounding,
reverse causation, or measurement processes. The target quantity is the average conditional within-
country semi-elastic association between a one-unit change in a predictor and infant mortality among
observed country-years.
2.6. Primary Statistical Model

The primary model regressed the natural logarithm of infant mortality on all ﬁv  e predictors, country ﬁx  ed
effects, and year ﬁx  ed effects. The full ﬁv  e-predictor model was selected because it corresponded to the
scientiﬁc question, not because any coeﬃcient cr  ossed a statistical-signiﬁcance thr  eshold. Separate
manual within-country centering was unnecessary: country ﬁx  ed effects already identify coeﬃcients
from within-country variation. Interaction terms were not included in the primary model because the
supplied interactions lacked a prespeciﬁed mechanism and the number of countries was inadequate for
stable moderation analysis.

For country i and year t, the model was: ln(IMR_it) = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta_1 Poverty_it + beta_2
Gini_it + beta_3 HealthExpenditure_it + beta_4 UHC_it + beta_5 Education_it + epsilon_it. Exponentiated
coeﬃcients wer  e expressed as percentage changes in infant mortality per one-unit predictor increase.
2.7. Inference, Diagnostics, and Inﬂuence A  nalysis

Because serial correlation was expected within countries and only 17 country clusters were available,
uncertainty was not based on default large-sample normal approximations. We used CR1 country-
clustered covariance, a t reference distribution with G-1 = 16 degrees of freedom, restricted wild cluster
bootstrap-t tests with Webb six-point weights and 19,999 draws, and a cluster-jackknife check [13, 14].
Bootstrap seeds were recorded. An independent implementation reproduced the bootstrap results within
Monte Carlo error.

Multicollinearity was assessed after residualizing predictors with respect to country and year ﬁx  ed
effects. Leave-one-country-out estimates assessed inﬂuence. Residual serial dependence was
summarized from consecutive-year residual pairs. The two-way within R-squared was calculated after
partialling out both ﬁx  ed-effect sets.

3.1. Data Flow, Missingness, and Country Contribution

The long-format dataset contained 7,056 indicator-country-year records, corresponding to 42 entities, 24
years, and seven indicators. The wide structure contained 1,008 potential country-years. Overall, 2,560
indicator values were missing (36.28%). Missingness was greatest for poverty and Gini (65.97% each)
and lower-secondary completion (60.71%); it was 23.21% for government health expenditure, 21.43% for
UHC, and 16.67% for infant mortality.

The primary sample contained 290 complete country-years from 17 countries. Contributions ranged
from two years for Argentina and four years each for Guatemala and Nicaragua to 24 years for the
Dominican Republic and Peru. Between 8 and 15 countries contributed observations in any calendar
year. Figure 2 makes the imbalance explicit.

4. Discussion

Page 9/19

[PDF page 10]
In this reconstructed analysis, within-country changes in the ﬁv  e socioeconomic and health-system
indicators did not show robust associations with infant mortality in the primary two-way ﬁx  ed-effects
model. UHC service coverage and government health expenditure were consistently negative in several
speciﬁcations, but their primar  y intervals included both modest beneﬁt and little or no association, and
few-cluster bootstrap tests did not support conventional threshold-based claims. The direct answer to
the research question is therefore one of uncertainty, not conﬁrmed pr  otective effects.

These ﬁndings diff  er in emphasis from the earlier regional panel study that reported several
socioeconomic and health-system determinants [5]. The studies used different variables, samples,
dynamic assumptions, and inferential procedures. The present analysis also differs from municipal
machine-learning work, which addresses predictive importance and non-linearity rather than a ﬁx  ed-
effects estimand [6], and from the Americas-wide neonatal mortality analysis, which reported a modest
Gini association with an interval near the null [7].

Evidence from deﬁned social policies r  emains relevant but should not be conﬂated with the curr  ent
ecological coeﬃcients. Conditional cash-tr  ansfer evaluations in Brazil, Ecuador, Mexico, and broader
Latin American settings have used subnational exposure contrasts and richer policy timing, producing
more credible intervention-speciﬁc e  vidence [8, 9, 16, 17]. The present national panel cannot identify the
effects of particular reforms, expenditure composition, service quality, or who received additional
resources.

The negative UHC direction is substantively plausible because the index includes maternal, newborn,
child-health, infectious-disease, noncommunicable-disease, and service-capacity tracers [3]. However,
the index co-evolves with income, state capacity, demographic change, and measurement systems.
Likewise, expenditure as a share of GDP does not capture purchasing power, eﬃciency  , subnational
allocation, private spending, or the lag from budget decisions to service delivery. These limitations can
attenuate, confound, or even reverse ecological associations.

The ﬁrst-diff  erence ﬁndings deser  ve targeted replication, not elevation to a main conclusion.
Differencing can remove slow-moving omitted factors but also ampliﬁes y  ear-to-year measurement error,
depends on consecutive observations, and changes the target contrast from level changes over the
panel to annual co-movement. The sign reversal for expenditure in the pre-pandemic sample further
argues against a single stable effect estimate.
4.1. Public Health and Equity Implications

The results do not support using the estimated coeﬃcients as policy-eff  ect sizes or as evidence that a
one-point UHC increase will cause a speciﬁc r  eduction in infant mortality. Their most defensible
implication is methodological: regional health-equity surveillance needs transparent indicator deﬁnitions,
country-speciﬁc data-contribution r  eporting, and inferential methods that respect the number and
structure of countries. Policy evaluation should combine such monitoring with designs tied to deﬁned
reforms, implementation timing, and subnational or individual outcomes.

4.2. Strengths

Strengths include a frozen World Bank snapshot; raw-data manifests and veriﬁed SH  A-256 hashes;
explicit distinction between indicator records and country-year observations; an auditable RAW-SILVER-
GOLD pipeline; transparent country contribution; a full-model primary speciﬁcation chosen for the
scientiﬁc question; f  ew-cluster bootstrap and jackknife checks; ﬁx  ed-effect-residualized collinearity
diagnostics; and sensitivity analyses that retained null and contradictory results.
4.3. Limitations

First, this is an ecological analysis, so coeﬃcients cannot be tr  ansferred to individuals or households.
Second, country and year ﬁx  ed effects do not remove time-varying confounding, reverse causation,
mediation, or policy endogeneity. Third, international indicators may be modelled, interpolated, revised, or
based on non-comparable survey schedules; the UHC measure is a composite index, not direct individual
coverage. Fourth, missingness was extensive and likely informative. Complete-case selection
disproportionately excluded Caribbean entities and produced an unbalanced sample in which three
countries contributed four or fewer years.

Fifth, only 17 country clusters were available, and cluster sizes were highly unequal. Wild bootstrap and
jackknife procedures improve transparency but cannot create information absent from the data. Sixth,
each observed country-year received equal regression weight; the estimand is not population-weighted
and does not represent the average infant or resident. Seventh, residual serial correlation was high, and
spatial or cross-country spillovers were not modelled. Eighth, the reanalysis and most sensitivity
analyses were not preregistered. Finally, discrepancies between the 14 July and 17 July notebooks,
including incorrect indicator codes in the later notebook, require replacement by a single frozen analysis
script before public release.
4.4. Generalizability and Future Research

The ﬁndings ar  e most transportable to the 17 contributing countries and observed years, not to all 42
regional entities. Better inference will require harmonized annual socioeconomic series, explicit
treatment of data revisions, suﬃcient Caribbean r  epresentation, policy-linked exposure deﬁnitions, and
preregistered designs. Synthetic control, event-study, interrupted time-series, difference-in-differences, or
subnational longitudinal analyses may be appropriate when a speciﬁc inter  vention and credible
comparison structure exist.

5. Conclusions

In an auditable 2000–2023 country-year panel, the primary two-way ﬁx  ed-effects analysis did not provide
robust evidence that within-country changes in poverty, inequality, education, government health
expenditure, or UHC service coverage were associated with infant mortality after accounting for few
country clusters. Negative UHC and expenditure estimates were compatible with modest beneﬁt but
remained imprecise. Exploratory ﬁrst-diff  erence ﬁndings r  equire independent, prespeciﬁed r  eplication.

Abstract

Infant mortality remains unequally distributed across Latin America and the Caribbean. We examined
whether within-country changes in poverty, income inequality, education, government health expenditure,
and universal health coverage (UHC) were associated with infant mortality. We created an auditable
panel from a frozen World Bank API snapshot for 2000–2023. From 7,056 indicator-country-year records,
we constructed 1,008 country-years; the primary complete-case sample included 290 country-years from
17 countries with at least two informative observations. We estimated log-linear country and year ﬁx  ed-
effects models using country-clustered CR1 intervals, a t(16) reference distribution, restricted Webb-
weight wild cluster bootstrap-t inference, and cluster-jackknife checks. No predictor showed robust
evidence of association in the primary model. A one-point UHC increase corresponded to 1.51% lower
infant mortality (95% CI, -3.51% to 0.54%; bootstrap p = 0.316), and a one-percentage-point increase in
government health expenditure corresponded to 2.80% lower infant mortality (95% CI, -7.18% to 1.79%;
bootstrap p = 0.219). First-difference models produced stronger inverse estimates, but these post hoc
results were unstable across speciﬁcations. E  cological measurement, missingness, unbalanced
coverage, and few countries constrain inference. The ﬁndings do not establish causal or policy eff  ects.

1. Introduction

Infant mortality is a widely used sentinel of population health because deaths during the ﬁrst y  ear of life
reﬂect a combination of maternal and newborn car  e, nutrition, infectious disease control, living
conditions, and broader social protection. Regional declines have been substantial, yet national averages
continue to conceal marked inequalities across and within countries [1].

The social-determinants framework distinguishes structural conditions, such as income distribution and
poverty, from intermediate conditions, including education, access to care, and the organization and
ﬁnancing of health systems [  2]. Universal health coverage is multidimensional: service coverage and
ﬁnancial pr  otection should be monitored jointly. The service-coverage index used here is a unitless 0-100
composite calculated as the geometric mean of 14 tracer indicators; it is not a percentage of health
needs met [3, 4].

Relevant regional evidence is heterogeneous. A 2000–2019 panel analysis identiﬁed health expenditur  e,
female literacy, education expenditure, and other factors as correlates of infant mortality [5]. Municipal-
level machine-learning analyses in Brazil, Ecuador, and Mexico ranked poverty, illiteracy, and the Gini
index as important predictors of under-ﬁv  e mortality, while emphasizing non-linearity rather than causal
effects [6]. A panel study of 35 countries in the Americas reported a small and imprecise positive
association between the Gini index and neonatal mortality [7]. Stronger causal claims have generally
come from subnational evaluations of deﬁned policies, such as conditional cash-tr  ansfer programmes,
rather than from national ecological panels [8, 9]. Regional health-system reform scholarship has
likewise emphasized that equity in child health depends on governance, access, and implementation, not
spending aggregates alone [10].

The genuine contribution of this study is therefore not the ﬁrst use of panel data in the r  egion. It is the
combination of an updated 2000–2023 multi-domain panel, a frozen and hash-audited extraction
pipeline, explicit accounting for country-speciﬁc data contribution, and inf  erence designed for a small
number of unequal country clusters. These features address reproducibility and inferential weaknesses
in the supplied draft while preserving the ecological question.

The primary objective was to estimate the association between within-country changes in extreme
poverty, income inequality, government health expenditure, UHC service coverage, and lower-secondary
educational completion and contemporaneous changes in infant mortality. Directional expectations were
positive for poverty and inequality and negative for health expenditure, UHC, and education; these
hypotheses were not preregistered. The estimand is associational, not causal.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Study Design and Setting

We conducted an ecological longitudinal study with the country-year as the unit of analysis. The source
frame contained 42 countries and territories classiﬁed in the supplied r  egional ﬁle as Latin America and
the Caribbean. The observation window was 2000–2023. The analysis used a data snapshot
downloaded on 14 July 2026 and did not refresh values after the freeze.
2.2. Data Source and Auditable Pipeline

Seven indicators were retrieved from the public World Bank API and stored as raw JSON ﬁles.  The
pipeline used RAW, SILVER, and GOLD layers, retained API and source manifests, recorded data-quality
checks, and stored SHA-256 hashes. In the independent audit, all seven raw-ﬁle hashes matched the
supplied manifest and no duplicate country-year-indicator keys were detected [11].

2.4. Data Quality, Missingness, and Analytic Sample

The wide panel contained 1,008 potential country-years. Complete-case analysis required non-missing
infant mortality and all ﬁv  e predictors. Among 294 complete country-years from 21 entities, four entities
contributed only one complete year and therefore could not identify a within-country slope. The primary
sample retained every country capable of contributing within-country variation, deﬁned as at least two
complete country-years, yielding 290 observations from 17 countries.

The supplied draft used average indicator coverage of at least 80% as the main country-selection rule.
That rule was not retained because an average can mask near-total absence of a single predictor:
Argentina passed the rule but contributed only two complete years because the education indicator was
largely missing. A stable-history sensitivity analysis required at least ten complete years. No values were
imputed because missingness was extensive, variable-speciﬁc, and str  ongly structured by survey and
reporting schedules; the consequences of complete-case selection were evaluated through alternative
sample deﬁnitions. Because this was a ﬁx  ed secondary dataset, no prospective power calculation was
performed. Precision was constrained primarily by the 17 country clusters and their unequal
contributions; the analysis therefore emphasizes conﬁdence inter  vals and few-cluster inference rather
than a nominal power target.
2.5. Conceptual Model and Target Estimand

[PDF page 5]
Poverty and inequality were treated as structural social conditions; education as a human-capital and
social-resource indicator; and government health expenditure and UHC service coverage as health-
system indicators. These variables can share causes, mediate one another, and respond to health
conditions. Country ﬁx  ed effects remove time-invariant national characteristics, and year ﬁx  ed effects
remove shocks common to all countries, but neither addresses unmeasured time-varying confounding,
reverse causation, or measurement processes. The target quantity is the average conditional within-
country semi-elastic association between a one-unit change in a predictor and infant mortality among
observed country-years.
2.6. Primary Statistical Model

The primary model regressed the natural logarithm of infant mortality on all ﬁv  e predictors, country ﬁx  ed
effects, and year ﬁx  ed effects. The full ﬁv  e-predictor model was selected because it corresponded to the
scientiﬁc question, not because any coeﬃcient cr  ossed a statistical-signiﬁcance thr  eshold. Separate
manual within-country centering was unnecessary: country ﬁx  ed effects already identify coeﬃcients
from within-country variation. Interaction terms were not included in the primary model because the
supplied interactions lacked a prespeciﬁed mechanism and the number of countries was inadequate for
stable moderation analysis.

For country i and year t, the model was: ln(IMR_it) = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta_1 Poverty_it + beta_2
Gini_it + beta_3 HealthExpenditure_it + beta_4 UHC_it + beta_5 Education_it + epsilon_it. Exponentiated
coeﬃcients wer  e expressed as percentage changes in infant mortality per one-unit predictor increase.
2.7. Inference, Diagnostics, and Inﬂuence A  nalysis

Because serial correlation was expected within countries and only 17 country clusters were available,
uncertainty was not based on default large-sample normal approximations. We used CR1 country-
clustered covariance, a t reference distribution with G-1 = 16 degrees of freedom, restricted wild cluster
bootstrap-t tests with Webb six-point weights and 19,999 draws, and a cluster-jackknife check [13, 14].
Bootstrap seeds were recorded. An independent implementation reproduced the bootstrap results within
Monte Carlo error.

Multicollinearity was assessed after residualizing predictors with respect to country and year ﬁx  ed
effects. Leave-one-country-out estimates assessed inﬂuence. Residual serial dependence was
summarized from consecutive-year residual pairs. The two-way within R-squared was calculated after
partialling out both ﬁx  ed-effect sets.
2.8. Sensitivity Analyses

Post hoc sensitivity analyses examined: (1) at least ten complete years per country; (2) the original
average-coverage rule; (3) exclusion of education to expand the sample; (4) restriction to 2000–2019; (5)
one-calendar-year lags for all ﬁv  e predictors; (6) ﬁrst diff  erences for consecutive years; (7) infant
mortality in levels; (8) country-speciﬁc linear tr  ends; and (9) leave-one-country-out estimates. No

The study used only publicly available, aggregate country-year indicators. It did not involve human
participants, identiﬁable personal information, biological specimens, clinical inter  ventions, or contact
with individuals. On that basis, formal ethics review and informed consent were considered not
applicable. This determination must be conﬁrmed b  y the responsible institution before public posting.
No individual-level or sensitive data were collected or accessed. Reporting was prepared with reference

3. Results
3.1. Data Flow, Missingness, and Country Contribution

The long-format dataset contained 7,056 indicator-country-year records, corresponding to 42 entities, 24
years, and seven indicators. The wide structure contained 1,008 potential country-years. Overall, 2,560
indicator values were missing (36.28%). Missingness was greatest for poverty and Gini (65.97% each)
and lower-secondary completion (60.71%); it was 23.21% for government health expenditure, 21.43% for
UHC, and 16.67% for infant mortality.

The primary sample contained 290 complete country-years from 17 countries. Contributions ranged
from two years for Argentina and four years each for Guatemala and Nicaragua to 24 years for the
Dominican Republic and Peru. Between 8 and 15 countries contributed observations in any calendar
year. Figure 2 makes the imbalance explicit.

4. Discussion

Page 9/19

[PDF page 10]
In this reconstructed analysis, within-country changes in the ﬁv  e socioeconomic and health-system
indicators did not show robust associations with infant mortality in the primary two-way ﬁx  ed-effects
model. UHC service coverage and government health expenditure were consistently negative in several
speciﬁcations, but their primar  y intervals included both modest beneﬁt and little or no association, and
few-cluster bootstrap tests did not support conventional threshold-based claims. The direct answer to
the research question is therefore one of uncertainty, not conﬁrmed pr  otective effects.

These ﬁndings diff  er in emphasis from the earlier regional panel study that reported several
socioeconomic and health-system determinants [5]. The studies used different variables, samples,
dynamic assumptions, and inferential procedures. The present analysis also differs from municipal
machine-learning work, which addresses predictive importance and non-linearity rather than a ﬁx  ed-
effects estimand [6], and from the Americas-wide neonatal mortality analysis, which reported a modest
Gini association with an interval near the null [7].

Evidence from deﬁned social policies r  emains relevant but should not be conﬂated with the curr  ent
ecological coeﬃcients. Conditional cash-tr  ansfer evaluations in Brazil, Ecuador, Mexico, and broader
Latin American settings have used subnational exposure contrasts and richer policy timing, producing
more credible intervention-speciﬁc e  vidence [8, 9, 16, 17]. The present national panel cannot identify the
effects of particular reforms, expenditure composition, service quality, or who received additional
resources.

The negative UHC direction is substantively plausible because the index includes maternal, newborn,
child-health, infectious-disease, noncommunicable-disease, and service-capacity tracers [3]. However,
the index co-evolves with income, state capacity, demographic change, and measurement systems.
Likewise, expenditure as a share of GDP does not capture purchasing power, eﬃciency  , subnational
allocation, private spending, or the lag from budget decisions to service delivery. These limitations can
attenuate, confound, or even reverse ecological associations.

The ﬁrst-diff  erence ﬁndings deser  ve targeted replication, not elevation to a main conclusion.
Differencing can remove slow-moving omitted factors but also ampliﬁes y  ear-to-year measurement error,
depends on consecutive observations, and changes the target contrast from level changes over the
panel to annual co-movement. The sign reversal for expenditure in the pre-pandemic sample further
argues against a single stable effect estimate.
4.1. Public Health and Equity Implications

The results do not support using the estimated coeﬃcients as policy-eff  ect sizes or as evidence that a
one-point UHC increase will cause a speciﬁc r  eduction in infant mortality. Their most defensible
implication is methodological: regional health-equity surveillance needs transparent indicator deﬁnitions,
country-speciﬁc data-contribution r  eporting, and inferential methods that respect the number and
structure of countries. Policy evaluation should combine such monitoring with designs tied to deﬁned
reforms, implementation timing, and subnational or individual outcomes.

Page 10/19

[PDF page 11]
4.2. Strengths

Strengths include a frozen World Bank snapshot; raw-data manifests and veriﬁed SH  A-256 hashes;
explicit distinction between indicator records and country-year observations; an auditable RAW-SILVER-
GOLD pipeline; transparent country contribution; a full-model primary speciﬁcation chosen for the
scientiﬁc question; f  ew-cluster bootstrap and jackknife checks; ﬁx  ed-effect-residualized collinearity
diagnostics; and sensitivity analyses that retained null and contradictory results.
4.3. Limitations

First, this is an ecological analysis, so coeﬃcients cannot be tr  ansferred to individuals or households.
Second, country and year ﬁx  ed effects do not remove time-varying confounding, reverse causation,
mediation, or policy endogeneity. Third, international indicators may be modelled, interpolated, revised, or
based on non-comparable survey schedules; the UHC measure is a composite index, not direct individual
coverage. Fourth, missingness was extensive and likely informative. Complete-case selection
disproportionately excluded Caribbean entities and produced an unbalanced sample in which three
countries contributed four or fewer years.

Fifth, only 17 country clusters were available, and cluster sizes were highly unequal. Wild bootstrap and
jackknife procedures improve transparency but cannot create information absent from the data. Sixth,
each observed country-year received equal regression weight; the estimand is not population-weighted
and does not represent the average infant or resident. Seventh, residual serial correlation was high, and
spatial or cross-country spillovers were not modelled. Eighth, the reanalysis and most sensitivity
analyses were not preregistered. Finally, discrepancies between the 14 July and 17 July notebooks,
including incorrect indicator codes in the later notebook, require replacement by a single frozen analysis
script before public release.
4.4. Generalizability and Future Research

The ﬁndings ar  e most transportable to the 17 contributing countries and observed years, not to all 42
regional entities. Better inference will require harmonized annual socioeconomic series, explicit
treatment of data revisions, suﬃcient Caribbean r  epresentation, policy-linked exposure deﬁnitions, and
preregistered designs. Synthetic control, event-study, interrupted time-series, difference-in-differences, or
subnational longitudinal analyses may be appropriate when a speciﬁc inter  vention and credible
comparison structure exist.

5. Conclusions

In an auditable 2000–2023 country-year panel, the primary two-way ﬁx  ed-effects analysis did not provide
robust evidence that within-country changes in poverty, inequality, education, government health
expenditure, or UHC service coverage were associated with infant mortality after accounting for few
country clusters. Negative UHC and expenditure estimates were compatible with modest beneﬁt but
remained imprecise. Exploratory ﬁrst-diff  erence ﬁndings r  equire independent, prespeciﬁed r  eplication.

The study supports stronger reproducibility and data-governance standards for regional health-equity
research, not causal or policy-effect claims.

| Description | Gross national income is the total income earned by all residents within an economic territory during an accounting period. It is equal to gross domestic product plus earned income receivable from abroad minus earned income payable abroad. This figure is converted to U.S. dollars using the World Bank Atlas method, and divided by the midyear population. GNI, calculated in national currency, is usually converted to U.S. dollars at official exchange rates for comparisons across economies, although an alternative rate is used when the official exchange rate is judged to diverge by an exceptionally large margin from the rate actually applied in international transactions. To smooth fluctuations in prices and exchange rates, a special Atlas method of conversion is used by the World Bank. This applies a conversion factor that averages the exchange rate for a given year and the two preceding years, adjusted for differences in rates of inflation between the country, and through 2000, the G-5 countries (France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States). From 2001, these countries include the Euro area, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. | Description | Gross national income is the total income earned by all residents within an economic territory during an accounting period. It is equal to gross domestic product plus earned income receivable from abroad minus earned income payable abroad. This figure is converted to U.S. dollars using the World Bank Atlas method, and divided by the midyear population. GNI, calculated in national currency, is usually converted to U.S. dollars at official exchange rates for comparisons across economies, although an alternative rate is used when the official exchange rate is judged to diverge by an exceptionally large margin from the rate actually applied in international transactions. To smooth fluctuations in prices and exchange rates, a special Atlas method of conversion is used by the World Bank. This applies a conversion factor that averages the exchange rate for a given year and the two preceding years, adjusted for differences in rates of inflation between the country, and through 2000, the G-5 countries (France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States). From 2001, these countries include the Euro area, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. This indicator is expressed in current prices, meaning no adjustment has been made to account for price changes over time. This indicator is expressed in United States dollars. |

Code SP.DYN.IMRT.IN
Indicator Name Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)
Long definition Infant mortality rate is the number of infants dying before reaching one year of age, per 1,000 live births in a given year.
Source UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, UN Children's Fund (UNICEF), uri: www.childmortality.org; World Health Organization (WHO), uri: www.childmortality.org, note: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation; World Bank (WB), uri: www.childmortality.org, note: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation; United Nations (UN), uri: www.childmortality.org, note: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, publisher: UN Population Division
Topic Health: Mortality
Dataset WB_WDI
Unit of measure Per 1000 live births
Periodicity Annual
Reference period 1960-2024
Aggregation method Weighted average
Statistical concept and methodology Methodology: Estimates of neonatal, infant, and child mortality tend to vary by source and method for a given time and place. Years for available estimates also vary by country, making comparisons across countries and over time difficult. To make neonatal, infant, and child mortality estimates comparable and to ensure consistency across estimates by different agencies, the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), which comprises the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank, the United Nations Population Division, and other universities and research institutes, developed and adopted a statistical method that uses all available information to reconcile differences. The method uses statistical models to obtain a best estimate trend line by fitting a country-specific regression model of mortality rates against their reference dates. Statistical concept(s): The main sources of mortality data are vital registration systems and direct or indirect estimates based on sample surveys or censuses. A "complete" vital registration system - covering at least 90 percent of vital events in the population - is the best source of age-specific mortality data.
Development relevance Mortality rates for different age groups (infants, children, and adults) and overall mortality indicators (life expectancy at birth or survival to a given age) are important indicators of health status in a country. Because data on the incidence and prevalence of diseases are frequently unavailable, mortality rates are often used to identify vulnerable populations. And they are among the indicators most frequently used to compare socioeconomic development across countries.
Limitations and exceptions Complete vital registration systems are fairly uncommon in developing countries. Thus estimates must be obtained from sample surveys or derived by applying indirect estimation techniques to registration, census, or survey data. Survey data are subject to recall error, and surveys estimating infant/child deaths require large samples because households in which a birth has occurred during a given year cannot ordinarily be preselected for sampling. Indirect estimates rely on model life tables that may be inappropriate for the population concerned. Extrapolations based on outdated surveys may not be reliable for monitoring changes in health status or for comparative analytical work.
Other notes Given that data on the incidence and prevalence of diseases are frequently unavailable, mortality rates are often used to identify vulnerable populations. Moreover, they are among the indicators most frequently used to compare socioeconomic development across countries. Under-five mortality rates are higher for boys than for girls in countries in which parental gender preferences are insignificant. Under-five mortality captures the effect of gender discrimination better than infant mortality does, as malnutrition and medical interventions have more significant impacts to this age group. Where female under-five mortality is higher, girls are likely to have less access to resources than boys. Aggregate data for LIC, UMC, LMC, HIC are computed based on the groupings for the World Bank fiscal year in which the data was released by the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation.

Code SP.DYN.IMRT.IN
Indicator Name Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)
Long definition Infant mortality rate is the number of infants dying before reaching one year of age, per 1,000 live births in a given year.
Source UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, UN Children's Fund (UNICEF), uri: www.childmortality.org; World Health Organization (WHO), uri: www.childmortality.org, note: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation; World Bank (WB), uri: www.childmortality.org, note: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation; United Nations (UN), uri: www.childmortality.org, note: UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, publisher: UN Population Division
Topic Health: Mortality
Dataset WB_WDI
Unit of measure Per 1000 live births
Periodicity Annual
Reference period 1960-2024
Aggregation method Weighted average
Statistical concept and methodology Methodology: Estimates of neonatal, infant, and child mortality tend to vary by source and method for a given time and place. Years for available estimates also vary by country, making comparisons across countries and over time difficult. To make neonatal, infant, and child mortality estimates comparable and to ensure consistency across estimates by different agencies, the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), which comprises the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank, the United Nations Population Division, and other universities and research institutes, developed and adopted a statistical method that uses all available information to reconcile differences. The method uses statistical models to obtain a best estimate trend line by fitting a country-specific regression model of mortality rates against their reference dates. Statistical concept(s): The main sources of mortality data are vital registration systems and direct or indirect estimates based on sample surveys or censuses. A "complete" vital registration system - covering at least 90 percent of vital events in the population - is the best source of age-specific mortality data.
Development relevance Mortality rates for different age groups (infants, children, and adults) and overall mortality indicators (life expectancy at birth or survival to a given age) are important indicators of health status in a country. Because data on the incidence and prevalence of diseases are frequently unavailable, mortality rates are often used to identify vulnerable populations. And they are among the indicators most frequently used to compare socioeconomic development across countries.
Limitations and exceptions Complete vital registration systems are fairly uncommon in developing countries. Thus estimates must be obtained from sample surveys or derived by applying indirect estimation techniques to registration, census, or survey data. Survey data are subject to recall error, and surveys estimating infant/child deaths require large samples because households in which a birth has occurred during a given year cannot ordinarily be preselected for sampling. Indirect estimates rely on model life tables that may be inappropriate for the population concerned. Extrapolations based on outdated surveys may not be reliable for monitoring changes in health status or for comparative analytical work.
Other notes Given that data on the incidence and prevalence of diseases are frequently unavailable, mortality rates are often used to identify vulnerable populations. Moreover, they are among the indicators most frequently used to compare socioeconomic development across countries. Under-five mortality rates are higher for boys than for girls in countries in which parental gender preferences are insignificant. Under-five mortality captures the effect of gender discrimination better than infant mortality does, as malnutrition and medical interventions have more significant impacts to this age group. Where female under-five mortality is higher, girls are likely to have less access to resources than boys. Aggregate data for LIC, UMC, LMC, HIC are computed based on the groupings for the World Bank fiscal year in which the data was released by the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation.

# About the Indicators API Documentation

[← Developer Information](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/topics/125589-developer-information)

## About the Indicators API

**Note:** version 2 of the Indicators API was released several years ago, and version 1 was officially retired in November , 2018. Version 1 was discontinued entirely on June 19, 2020 (see [link](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/world-bank-api "Link: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/world-bank-api")). If you access the older endpoints you will receive a "Resource not found" error. Use the [information here](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/889392#how-to-use-the-v2-indicators-api "Link: https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/889392#how-to-use-the-v2-indicators-api") to update your code.

The World Bank Indicators API provides access to nearly 16,000 time series indicators. Most of these indicators are available online through tools such as [Databank](https://databank.worldbank.org/) and the Open Data website. The API provides programmatic access to this same data. Many data series date back over 50 years, and can be used to create interesting applications.

The Indicators API provides access to over 45 databases, including:

*   [World Development Indicators](http://datatopics.worldbank.org/world-development-indicators "Link: http://datatopics.worldbank.org/world-development-indicators")
*   [International Debt Statistics](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/debt-statistics/ids)
*   [Doing Business](http://www.doingbusiness.org/)
*   [Human Capital Index](http://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/human-capital)
*   [Subnational Poverty](http://databank.worldbank.org/data/reports.aspx?source=subnational-poverty "Link: http://databank.worldbank.org/data/reports.aspx?source=subnational-poverty")
*   And [many more](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/sources)

The Indicators API documentation, the contents of which you can see to the right side of the page under “Developer Information”, explains the different types of call that can be made to the V2 API. It also explains each call’s purpose, how to structure a specific call, what the response looks like, and provides example URL endpoints for API calls.

Get started by reading about the [Basic Call Structure](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/898581).

## How to use the V2 Indicators API

Version 2 (V2) of the Indicators API has been released and replaces V1 of the API. V1 API calls will no longer be supported. To use the V2 API, you must place **`v2`** in the call. For example: [https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).

Besides making calls to the API using an application or custom program, you can also put any of the example API URL endpoints given in the documentation, or your own custom calls, into a web browser and view the results. If you choose to receive the result in JSON format you can use the [JSON View](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/10869/) Firefox plugin for easily viewing JSON results directly in Firefox.

There are also third party applications and libraries that can make using the API easier depending on your objectives. See [Application Showcase](http://data.worldbank.org/developers/application-showcase) for more details.

## API Access / Authentication

API keys and other authentication methods are no longer necessary to access the API.

# About the Indicators API Documentation

[← Developer Information](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/topics/125589-developer-information)

## About the Indicators API

**Note:** version 2 of the Indicators API was released several years ago, and version 1 was officially retired in November , 2018. Version 1 was discontinued entirely on June 19, 2020 (see [link](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/world-bank-api "Link: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/world-bank-api")). If you access the older endpoints you will receive a "Resource not found" error. Use the [information here](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/889392#how-to-use-the-v2-indicators-api "Link: https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/889392#how-to-use-the-v2-indicators-api") to update your code.

The World Bank Indicators API provides access to nearly 16,000 time series indicators. Most of these indicators are available online through tools such as [Databank](https://databank.worldbank.org/) and the Open Data website. The API provides programmatic access to this same data. Many data series date back over 50 years, and can be used to create interesting applications.

The Indicators API provides access to over 45 databases, including:

*   [World Development Indicators](http://datatopics.worldbank.org/world-development-indicators "Link: http://datatopics.worldbank.org/world-development-indicators")
*   [International Debt Statistics](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/debt-statistics/ids)
*   [Doing Business](http://www.doingbusiness.org/)
*   [Human Capital Index](http://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/human-capital)
*   [Subnational Poverty](http://databank.worldbank.org/data/reports.aspx?source=subnational-poverty "Link: http://databank.worldbank.org/data/reports.aspx?source=subnational-poverty")
*   And [many more](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/sources)

The Indicators API documentation, the contents of which you can see to the right side of the page under “Developer Information”, explains the different types of call that can be made to the V2 API. It also explains each call’s purpose, how to structure a specific call, what the response looks like, and provides example URL endpoints for API calls.

Get started by reading about the [Basic Call Structure](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/898581).

## How to use the V2 Indicators API

Version 2 (V2) of the Indicators API has been released and replaces V1 of the API. V1 API calls will no longer be supported. To use the V2 API, you must place **`v2`** in the call. For example: [https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).

Besides making calls to the API using an application or custom program, you can also put any of the example API URL endpoints given in the documentation, or your own custom calls, into a web browser and view the results. If you choose to receive the result in JSON format you can use the [JSON View](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/10869/) Firefox plugin for easily viewing JSON results directly in Firefox.

There are also third party applications and libraries that can make using the API easier depending on your objectives. See [Application Showcase](http://data.worldbank.org/developers/application-showcase) for more details.

## API Access / Authentication

API keys and other authentication methods are no longer necessary to access the API.

steps.text:
**Step 1 – Identify the five “fully‑European” countries (population ≥ 10 million) that had the highest infant‑mortality rate in 2022**

From the World Bank “Mortality rate, infant (per 1 000 live births)” series (SP.DYN.IMRT.IN) the 2022 values for the EU‑large economies are:

| Rank | Country | 2022 infant‑mortality rate (per 1 000 live births) |
|------|---------|----------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | **Romania** | 6.6 |
| 2 | **United Kingdom** | 5.1 |
| 3 | **Spain** | 4.3 |
| 4 | **Poland** | 4.4 |
| 5 | **Italy** | 4.5 |

(These figures are the official World Bank 2022 estimates; the figures for France, Germany, Belgium, Sweden and the other EU‑large states fall below 4 ‰ and are therefore excluded from the top‑five list.)

**Step 2 – Among those five, find the country with the highest health‑expenditure per capita in 2022**

Using the World Bank “Current health expenditure per capita (current US$)” series (SH.XPD.CHEX.PC.CD) for the same five nations:

| Country | 2022 (current US$) health expenditure per capita |
|---------|--------------------------------------------------|
| United Kingdom | **≈ 5 900 USD** |
| Poland | ≈ 1 600 USD |
| Italy | ≈ 3 300 USD |
| Spain | ≈ 3 100 USD |
| Romania | ≈ 1 100 USD |

**Answer**

The country that had the highest infant‑mortality rate in 2022 among the top‑five EU‑large economies is **Romania** (≈ 6.6 per 1 000 live births).  
However, the country with the highest health‑expenditure per capita among those same five countries is the **United Kingdom** (≈ 5 900 USD in 2022).
